Inter cropping
• Growing intercrops helps in effective utilization of soil, water and sun light.
• Annual intercrops like Turmeric, Zinger, Colacasia, Cabbage, Cauliflower, Beans,
Chillies, Brinjal and Bhendican be grown in young gardens upto 5 to 6 years of age from
planting.
• In old gardens above 20 years perennials like Banana, Cocoa, Pepper, Pineapple, Papaya,
Heliconia, etc. can be cultivated.
Irrigation:
Palm needs large quantities of water for satisfactory performance. Due to
irrigation, production of female flowers and setting percentage increase considerably.
Irrigation is more essential in light soils and areas of low rainfall and long spells.
Common method of irrigation is Basin and flood irrigation; when water is scarce drip
irrigation is to be provided. In rainfed coconuts mulching of basins is required. Surface
mulching with coconut leaves or farm waste and sowing of Green manure crops in the basins
also help in soil moisture retention.
Button shedding
Shedding of buttons and premature nuts in coconut may be due to any one of the
following reasons i.e., Excess acidity or alkalinity, Lack of drainage, Lack of nutrients, Lack
of pollination, Hormone deficiency, Pests and diseases and Genetic causes.
The following remedial measures are suggested for button shedding.
1. Rectification of soil pH: Excess acidity or alkalinity of soil may cause button shedding.
This could be rectified by adding lime or gypsum.
2. Providing adequate drainage facilities: Lack of drainage results in the roots of coconut
trees getting suffocated for want of aeration and shedding of buttons occur under such
condition. Drainage channels have to be dug to drain the excess water during rainy season.
3. Lack of nutrition: Button shedding occurs due to inadequate or lack of manuring. The
recommended dose of manurial schedules and proper time of application are important to
minimise the button shedding.
4. Lack of pollination: Button shedding also occurs due to lack of pollination. Setting up of
beehives @ 15 units/ha may increase the cross pollination in the garden. through honey,
increases the net profit per unit area.
5. Hormone deficiency: Button shedding also occurs due to hormone deficiency. By
spraying 2, 4- D at 30 ppm or NAA 20 ppm (2,4-D 30 mg or NAA 20 mg per litre of water)
on the inflorescence one month after opening of the spathe minimise the button shedding.
6. Pests and Diseases incidence: Button shedding also occurs due to attack of pests and
diseases. To control this, spray monocrotophos @ 1.6ml/L. Spray Blitox 3g/L water 2-3
times during monsoon
7. Genetic causes: In some trees button shedding may persist even after ensuring adequate
manuring, irrigation and crop pest and disease management. This is an indication of inherent
defect of the mother palm from which the seed material was obtained. This underlines the
need for proper choice of superior mother palm for collecting seed coconut to ensure
uniformly good yielding trees.
Harvesting:
Tall varieties start flowering in 5-7 years after planting and Dwarf varieties flower
in 3rd year. Once enters bearing stage, continuously produce flowering. 12 bunches are
expected per year. They take 11-13 months from flowering to maturity. Hallow sound on
tapping, brown colouration of husk are the maturity indices. However coconuts are harvested
at different ages for different purposes are as follows
Tender nuts 6-7 months old
Green husk 10-11months old
Copra and oil 11-12months old
Seed 12 months old
Monthly harvests are made for tender nuts. For copra and oil matured nuts are
harvested at 45 days interval during summer and 60 days interval during rainy season. 8 – 10
harvests are made per year. For seed only one harvest is taken per year.
Yield: Tall variety: 60-80 nuts under rainfed conditions. 80-100 nuts underirrigated
conditions.
Intercropping in Coconut gardens:
Since coconut is perennial in nature, since the market price for coconut is also fluctuates and
to utilize the available interspace and natural resources like water, sunlight cultivation of
intercrops is followed which generates additional income to the farmers and sustains the
income generation.
Generally, Multistoried cropping system is followed for better utilization of sunlight.
Annual crops: in coconut gardens of below five years age there is enough sunlight and air
circulation is available where it is possible to cultivate annual crops such as turmeric, ginger,
yams, cabbage, cauliflower, beans, cucurbits, chilli, brinjal, bhendi, pulses, ground nut are
cultivated.
Perennial crops: in gardens of more than 20 years age perennial crops like banana, coco,
pineapple, papaya, heliconia, pepper are cultivated which gives sustainable income.
In areas of water scarcity, light soils like red sandy soils moisture will remain for limited
period hence short duration crops like beans, maize, groundnut are grown.
Growing of green manure crops i.e., pillipesara, crotalaria, sunhemp enhances soil fertility.
Addition of manures and fertilizers for both the main crop and intercrops as per the
recommendation increases yield of both the crops.
Lecture 17
Importance of vegetable cultivation – nutritional values, importance of
vegetables in human nutrition
The branch of horticulture that deals with the cultivation of vegetables is known as
Olericulture. The word olericulture is derived from the Latin word Oleriswhich means pot
herb and the English word culture which means cultivation. Thus olericulture means
cultivation of pot herbs. However, in the present days, it is broadly used to indicate the
cultivation of vegetables.
The term vegetable is applied to the edible herbaceous plant or plant parts thereof,
which are consumed generally in the unripe stage after cooking.
The balanced diet contains adequate energy source, nutrients and vitamins, minerals,
carbohydrates, fats, protein, etc. Vegetable are the reliable source for many dietary factors.
As vegetables contain many of the dietary factors like vitamins, minerals and amino acids.
According to the ICMR/WHO, daily requirement of vegetables per head are 100 g tubers,
100 g leafy vegetables, 120 g other vegetables. India is the second largest vegetable
producing country after china though our productivity is less as compared to other countries
due to following reasons.
1. Non availability of High yielding varieties.
2. Extension services are limited which are not reaching to the needy farmers.
3. Non availability of systematic market.
4. Lack of storage facilities for vegetables.
Importance of vegetables in human nutrition:
Vegetables produce taste, increase appetite withadequate quantity of fibres. They
maintain good health and protect against degenerative diseases. They can neutralise the acids
produced during digestion of proteins and fats. Fruits and vegetables are recognized as
protective foods as they are the chief sources of vitamins, minerals, carbohydrates, fats,
proteins, etc. necessary for the maintenance of human health.
Vegetables rich in Vitamins and Minerals:
Vitamin-A:Deficiency leads to retarded growth in children, formation of stones in kidneys,
creates problem in breathing. Its deficiency causes night blindness.
Source: leafy greens, carrot, cabbage, tomato
Vitamin- B (Thaimine): Deficiency leads to loss of weight, lowers body temperature and
leads to digestion problems, mainly it causes Beriberi disease.
Source: legume seeds such as peas, beans
Vitamin- C (Ascorbic acid): its deficiency leads to scurvy disease and paucity of heart
muscles.
Source: Tomato, palak, menthi, cabbage, greenchillies, spinach, potatoes, peas and beans
and carrot.
Vitamin- D (Calciferol)/ Ricketic vitamin: This vitamin is necessary for building up of
bones, preventing rickets and diseases of teeth.
Source: All green leafy vegetables are rich in vitamin D.
Vitamin- E (Tocopherol): This vitamin is also known as Anti –sterility. It has an important
effect on the generative functions and promotes fertility.
Source: Green lettuce and other green vegetables.
Vitamin- k (Pyridoxin): This vitamin prevents blood clotting
Source: All green leafy vegetables are rich in this vitamin.
Proteins:Proteins are essential for the growth of the body. Deficiency of proteinscauses
retarded growth and increased susceptibility to diseases and causes lethargy.
Source:Peas and beans are rich in proteins.
Carbohydrates: These are essential for supply energy.
Source: Potatoes, Sweet potato.
Minerals: Human body requires minerals like P, Ca, Iron, and Iodine etc. leafy greens are
rich in Ca and Fe.
Lecture 18
Vegetable gardens – kitchen gardens – vegetables gardens according to
purpose/ situations
According to the purpose of vegetables cultivation, vegetable gardens are classified into
two types:
1. Kitchen gardens
2. Vegetable gardens for commercial purpose (these are again classified as five types)
1. Market gardens
2. Transport gardens
3. Vegetable forcing
4. Gardens for processing units
5. Gardens for seed production
Objectives of Kitchen gardens: These vegetable gardens are mainly meant for growing and
supplying of fresh vegetables to meet the daily requirement of the family.
Advantages of kitchen garden:
✓ best means of recreation and exercise.
✓ An excellent hobby and healthy occupation for young and old during their
leisure time.
✓ Cut down the expenditure on purchase of vegetables.
✓ Vegetables grown in kitchen garden are fresh and are free from market
infection.
Kitchen gardens, where vegetable crops are grown in the backyard of a house or any
available space in the home compound by engaging the family members to produce fresh and
nutritionally rich vegetables which are free from pesticide residues as compared to the
vegetables available in outside markets. This type of gardens also gives immense opportunity
to children for learning about vegetable cultivation which creates enthusiasm.
Important points to be considered in laying of kitchen gardens:
1. All the stubbles, stones, broken glass pieces in the site should be removed before
leveling. Addition of 2.5 kg Compost, 50 g Super phosphate, 25 g Ammonium
sulphate, 125 g Potash fertilizers to be done before leveling the land. Urea @ 50 g is
to applied in 2-3 split doses during the entire growth of the crop.
2. An area of 2m x1mis allotted at one corner to prepare raised (15 cm height) nursery
beds for the vegetables like tomato, brinjal, chilli, cabbage, cauliflower. These
seedlings are to be transplanted at 5-6 week age.
3. Perennial trees like banana, lemon, curry leaf, drumstick should be planted in north
direction to avoid shade effect on other vegetables.
4. During summer and rainy season, on three sides of fence cucurbit vegetables like
ridge gourd, bottle gourd, cucumber, snake gourd, bitter gourd to be trained while in
winter season beans to be trained on fourth side.
5. The place along the bund side should be used to grow tuber and root crops (Carrot,
Colacasia, Radish, Beet root).
6. Short duration leafy vegetables like spinach, fenugreek, coriander, lettuce can be
grown in between the rows of long duration vegetables like cabbage, cauliflower etc.
7. Compost pits are prepared on one corner side to dump all the kitchen waste so as to
prepare manure for the kitchen garden.
8. A plan should be prepared well in advance according to the season and the total area
should be divided into small plots so that vegetables can be grown throughout the
year.
9. Generally, rectangular site should be preferred to kitchen gardens.
10. Planting should be done according to their maturity, the early maturing types should
be planted at one side to utilize the place afterwards.
11. Fertilizer application and Irrigation should be given timely and whenever it requires.
12. Always it is necessary to take pure and quality seed or planting material and thus
should match with the growing season.
13. Regular monitoring of pest and disease is necessary to take plant protection.
Commercial vegetable gardens:
1.Market gardens: Market gardens produce vegetables for local markets and theseare
located within 10-20 km from a city. Selection of vegetables to be produced depends on the
demand of local market. A market gardener will like to grow early varieties to catch the early
market. Returns are high in this gardens as intensive method is followed, land and labour cost
is compensated by the availability of city compost, sludge and water.
2. Truck gardens: A truck-garden produces one or two selected crops in a relatively large
quantity for distant markets. It generally follows a more extensive method of cultivation than
the market-garden. The cost of labour and land may cheap and he follows mechanized
method of cultivation, hence his cost of cultivation is less. The net income is also less as this
includes cost of transport and charges of middlemen.
3. Gardens for vegetable forcing: Main aim of these gardens is the production of vegetables
out of the normal season (Off season production). These can be grown in protected structures
by creating suitable environment for the selected crop. Quality of the produce is good and it
fetches high price.
4. Vegetable garden for processing:Vegetable garden for processing develops around the
processing factories and is mainly responsible for supplying vegetables to the factories
regularly. This type of garden grows particular varieties suitable for canning, dehydration or
freezing.These gardens specialized in growing only a few vegetables in bulk.
Ex: Tomato. Potato
5. Vegetable garden for seed production: The main purpose of these gardens is seed
production. The gardener should have a thorough knowledge of a vegetable in respect of its
growth habits, mode of pollination, proper isolation distance, cleaning, threshing, grading etc.
in the production of quality seed. Therefore, it is considered as a special type of garden.

Lecture 20
Vegetable nurseries- seed treatment –management of raised nursery beds
Raising of vegetable seedlings play crucial role in the production of vegetables which
accounts for half of the profits. In developed countries, seedling production is taken up by
private companies. In recent years, quality seedling production is also gaining importance
among farming community to utilize the raised beds and protray nurseries on commercial
scale.
Crops like cucurbits, beans, French beans, bhendi, cluster bean, drum stick which
have bold seed can be sown directly. Whereas, in small seeded crops like tomato, brinjal,
cabbage, cauliflower, chilli, onion seedlings to be raised and transplanted in the main field.
Raising of vegetable nursery:
The land should get ample sunlight, aeration and near to irrigation source. It should be
ploughed 3-4 times to bring to fine tilth. 4 m length, 1 m width and 15 cm raised beds of 10
are sufficient to supply seedlings per one acre. Water stagnation and damping off of seedlings
can be prevented in raised beds.
During hot summer season, covering the beds with white polythene mulch for about
15 days kills fungal spores. Well decomposed Farm yard manure @ 40 kg is and 2 kg
Azospirillum or Azatobacter is applied per 40 m2 beds. Before sowing of seeds, beds should
be drenched with 1% Bordeaux mixture or 3 g Copper oxy Chloride. Seeds to be sown in 10
cm apart and 1-2 cm deep, thin sowing facilitate air circulation and healthy growth of the
seedlings. Watering is to be provided with rose cans regularly, beds should be covered with
paddy straw to protect from heavy rains during rainy season. After sprouting, straw should be
removed. Weeds should be removed regularly. 15 days after sprouting, Furadon 3G granules
@ 100 g is mixed with fine sand and applied in the beds. malathion or dimethoate 2 ml + 3 g
mancozeb is sprayed to control sucking pests and leaf spots. If any damping off is noticed,
drenching with COC @ 3 g per litre is to be done. Withholding of water is to done at least
one week before transplanting. Light watering is given 6-12 hours before pulling of
seedlings. To avoid pests and diseases incidence in main field, dipping of seedlings for about
20-80 min in 20 ml Dimethoate + 10 g Carbedazinm in 10 litrewater to be practiced. Once
the seedlings attain 4-5 weeks age, 8-10 cm height and 2-3 leaves are transplanted in main
field.
Seed treatment:Incidence of seed borne pathogens can be minimized by treating the seed
with insecticide or fungicide is necessary before sowing. Black rot in Cruciferous vegetables
and Phomopsis blight in brinjal can be controlled by soaking seed in hot water (500c) for
about 30 minutes thereafter seeds are shade dried. In chilli, seeds are treated with Trisodium
orthophosphate @ 150 g per litre of water for 30 min thereafter remove the seeds and
washed with fresh water and shade dried to control the virus infestation. For the control of the
sucking pests, seed treatment with Imidachloprid @ 8 g per kg of seed should be done
followed by treatment with Captan or Thiram 3 g per litre to control seed borne pathogens. In
crops like bhendi, tomato, beans, bottle gourd, ridge gourd, snake gourd seeds are treated
with Imidachloprid @ 5 g per kg of seed followed by Captan or Thiram 3 g per seed before
sowing. Seed treatment with Trichoderma viridae @ 4-5 g per kg seed prior to sowingis
necessary to control soil borne diseases.
Management of raised nursery beds:
• Avoid water stagnation in the selected site.
• pH of the soil is 6.5.
• Land should be ploughed 4-5 times and remove all the weeds, stubbles, dried roots
etc.
• To supply seedlings per one hectare, an area of 10 m x 15 m is sufficient to grow
nursery. Raised beds of 15 cm height, 9 m length and 1 width are prepared. In
between nursery beds a furrow or channel with 30 cm width and 10 cm depth should
be made to drain out excess water during rainy season.
• 15 kg of well decomposed farm yard manure 100 g of nitrogen, phosphorous and
potassium fertilizers are to be supplied to each bed.
• 100 g neem cake is mixed with 5 g Tricodermaviride powder for a square meter of
nursery bed.
• Nursery beds are drenched with 3 g Copper oxy chloride( COC) per litre water to
avoid damping off disease.
• Seeds should be sown in 5-8 cm apart in 1 cm depth.
• Mulching with paddy straw helps in generation of heat facilitates for hasten up the
germination and also prevents the seeds from eating away from ants.
• To protect the young seedlings from sucking pests spraying of Imidachloprid 0.2 ml
per litre of water after 7-10 days of emergence seeds should be done.
• Withholding of watering prior to transplanting will harden up the seedlings.
• To protect the beds from sucking pests it should be provided with 40 or 50 mesh
nylon nets.
• 2-3 days before pulling of the seedlings beds seedlings are to be sprayed with 2 ml
Dimethoate + Carbedazim to protect from pest and disease for a month in the main
field. (or) it can also be done that the seedlings are to be dipped for about 20 minutes
in the same solution before transplanting.
• seedlings are ready for transplanting in about 25-42 days based on the crop and
variety.
Use of nylon net: Healthy seedlings are essentialto get good quality as well as higher
yield. During the initial growth, pests and disease incidence results in poor quality and
reduced yields. It is necessary to use nylon nets of 40 or 50 mesh and these are
supported with bamboo or GI pipesto protect the young seedlings. An area of 150
sq.m is needed to grow seedlings required per one hectare which costs around Rs.
5000/-.
Solarization: If the nursery beds are exposed to direct sunlight, insect pupae, soil
pathogens can be killed. The beds are sun dried and covered with polythene sheet
which kills the pathogens and also reduces the weed growth.
Solarization is done by following ways:
• Nurserysoilis mixed with well decomposed farm yard manure.
• Nursery beds are drenched with water then covered with 200 gauge polythene
sheet.
• This has to be kept for about 30-40 days to raise the temperature of 520C
during summer.
• Care should be taken that the polythene sheet should not be damaged/tare.
Lecture 21
Cultivation of important vegetables - Tomato- varieties- soil –climate
Tomato
Scientific name: Solanum lycoprsicon
Family: Solanaceae
Tomato is the world's largest vegetable crop after potato and sweet potato and one of
the most important protective foods. The fruits are rich in vitamin C, vitamin B, vitamin A.
Both the matured as well as ripened fruits are used. Various bye products like pickles, sauce,
ketchup, soups are made out of fruits.
Climate:Tomato can be cultivated throughout the year though the good yields can be
obtained during winter. It is susceptible to high as well as low temperatures (>380C and < 10
0C) which adversely affect the fruiting yield and quality. Maximum fruit set occurs at a night
temperature of 15 to 200 C. At ripen stage, fruits develop a red pigment called Lycopene,
which is inhibited at high temperature.
Soil: Tomato can be grown in a wide range of soils from sandy to heavy soils. A well-
drained, fairly fertile loam with fair moisture holding capacity is ideal for growing a good
crop of tomato. Tomato is highly susceptible to water logging. Well drained soils are highly
necessary. The preferable pH range is 6 to 7.

Lecture 22
Tomato - manures and fertilizers- water management –inter
cultivation- deficiencies- pest and diseases – plant protection –
harvest – yield
Manures &Fertilizers: Well decomposed Farm Yard Manure of 6-8 ton per acre is applied
along with 24 kg each of Phosphorous and Potash and incorporated into soil. Nitrogen @ 48-
60kg is applied in 3 split doses at 30 days, 45 days and 60 days after transplanting. Incase of
hybrids additional 50 % above fertilizers are applied.
Micro nutrients like B, Zn also need to be applied @ 8-12 kg borax, 10 kg ZnsSO
4/
acre.Availability of Boran is considered to be essential for production of large size fruit with
high vitamin content and prevent fruit cracking, while Zinc for higher ascorbic acid content
and tolerance to diseases.
Irrigation:
Tomato is a deep rooted crop. Roots will grow to a depth of 120 to 150 cm and it has
some drought tolerance. They require adequate moisture for their fair growth. Excess as well
as insufficient moisture is harmful. First irrigation is given immediately after transplanting
thereafter light irrigation should be given at 3 to 4 days interval in summer 10 to 15 day
interval in winter.
Weeding:Pendimethalin 1.25 ml or alachlor 1 l (light soils), 1.25 l (heavy soils) or
Metribuzen 300 g per 200 l of water is sprayed on the entire ground to suppress weed growth.
The same dose of Metribuzen is again sprayed after 15 days of first spraying.
Intercultural operations:
Tomato is subjected to pinching, the lateral shoots are pinched to improve more bushy
growth but little foliage is to be kept. Frequent shallow hoeings are necessary to improve the
yield it also reduce the weed growth. Mulching should be done 15 to 20 days after planting.
Staking is very essential for indeterminate group of varieties because it improves yield and
quality of fruits.
Harvesting:
Harvesting isdepends upon the purpose for which they are used and the distance of
transportation. In general, it commences flowering after 65-70 days after planting. Fruits are
ready in about 45-60 days after flowering. Fruits at green stage are suitable for distant market
while red are suitable for local market and fully ripened will be sent to processing industries.
Yield: Rabi – 12-16 t /ac
Summer 8-12 t /ac
Storage: Tomatoes can be stored for 20 days at 12-15 0C whereas, fully ripened are stored for
10 days at 4.5 0C.

Cultivation practices of Brinjal
Botanical name: Solanummelongena
Family: Solanaceae
Brinjal is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables in India. It is rich in minerals is Ca,
Mg, P, K and Fe. It is a good source of Vitamin A and C. Bitterness in Brinjal is due to
presence of glycoalkaloids.
Climate:Brinjal is the warm season crop. It is susceptible to severe frost. It requires a long
warm season, before fruit maturity. Optimum temperature is 22 to 330C. Under very cool
seasonal conditions, the ovaries are split leading to the development of abnormal fruits.
Soil: Brinjal can be grown on a wide range of soils. The ideal soils should be a deep, fertile
and well drained. The pH should be not more than 5.5 to 6.5 for better growth and
development. Light soils are good for a healthy crop but heavy soils are suited for higher
yields.

Lecture 24
Cultivation practies of Bhendi

Bhendi is grown in tropical to subtropical regions. Fresh fruits have good market in
Gulf countries.
Uses: Fresh fruits are used for various preparations. Fruits are used to make fry, boiled and in
soups. Nutritionally, it is rich in Vitamin A, B, C. it contains higher amounts of Iodine which

crop also comes up well with good yield in fertile loamy soils. Suitable soil pH is 6.0 -6.8.

Lecture -25
Beans – Cultivation practices
All the beans and peas are belong to the family, Leguminaceae.
Characteristics of Leguminaceae family:
1. Plant habit is bush to pole nature. Susceptible to frost except garden pea which prefers cool
climate.
2. Beans prefer warm climate.
3. All the plants are annuals except Dolichus which is perennial.
4. Plants of this family fix atmospheric nitrogen in root nodules with the help of Rhizobium
bacteria.
5. All the crops in this family are self -pollinated types. Fruits are called as pods.
6. Nutritionally these are rich in protein. Also contains vitamin A, C, minerals like Ca, Fe, P.
Vegetables belong to Leguminaceae:
Beans – Dolichous lablab
French bean – Phaseolus vulgaris
Cluster bean – Cyamopsis tetragonoloba
Cowpea – Vigna unguculata
Lima bean – Phaseolus lunatus
Peas – Pisum sativum
Cultivation practices of beans:
Botanical name: Dolichus lablab
Tender pods are used as fresh vegetable and the dried seeds are used as pulse. It prefers warm
climate. Climber types are suitable for cultivation during Kharif season while bush types can
be cultivated both in summer as well as in Kharif season.
Soil: All type of soils are suitable for its cultivation with a pH 6.5 -8.5.
Varieties:
Pole types: Pusa Early Prolific, Depalival, Pusa Sem -2, Pusa Sem – 3.
1. RND -1: it is a Pole type with high yield. Commences to flowering 130-150 days after
sowing. Pods are 15-20 cm long and bear in clusters. Crop duration is 210-240 days
and yields 15-18 t/a.
Bush types:

Bush types – 1.5 -2 kg/ac

types are sown in Kharif during June-July, in Rabi during September – October and in

Seed should be treated with Rhizobium culture @ 200 g per one kg of seed. 2-3 seeds are

before commencement of sowing. NPK fertilizers in a ratio of 30- 24-12 kg per acre are
supplied. Among these fertilizers entire P, K and half of N are applied at the time last plough
and the remaining half N is applied 30 days after sowing. Irrigation is given immediately
after fertilizer application.
Intercultural operations: Regular weeding is done. Shallow cultivation is to be done at
early stages of crop growth. Earthing up around the base of the plant gives additional support
and encourages root growth.
Climbing varieties need supported of bamboo sticks. Single stick is fixed near each
plant.In pole types, once the tendrils are formed these are tied with a rope and trained to a
frame work consists of line of pairs of caves.
Irrigation: irrigation is given once in 7-10 days. Flowering and pod development stages are
critical for moisture stress.
Harvest: Pods are harvested at tender stage. Pods take 2-3 weeks after flowering.
Yield: Pod yield: 3.6 – 4 t/ac
Seed yield: 0.6-0.8 t/ac
Seed production: Maintain isolation distance of 50 m from other varieties for seed
production. Pods are harvested after maturing and pod colour turns to yellow and pods are
harvested to separate the seeds.
Lecture 26
French Bean and Cowpea– cultivation practices
Botanical name: Phaseolus vulgaris
Family :Leguminaseae
French bean is one of the important legumes grown in winter season. Tender pods are
used mainly in Biryani and cooked as a vegetable. Seeds are separated from the matured pods
and used as other pulses in culinary preparations. Dried seeds of French bean are called as
Rajma.
Climate: French bean is a cool season crop. It gives good yield under mild warm season. It
is sensitive to frost. Optimum temperature required for good growth is 15-210C. In our state,
it is mainly grown during winter season.
Soil:Sandy loams are best for its cultivation. Heavy soil gives good yield. Ideal pH range is
between 6 to 7. French bean mature early on sandy soils compared to other soils.
Varities:
1. Arkakomal:Plant is bushy. Early type. Yields 4.0-4.8t/ac.
2. Bountiful:Introduction from US comes up in September to February. It is resistant to
common diseases. Comes to first picking 70 days after sowing.
3. Contender:Tolerant to powdery mildew and mosaic. Bushy type and pods are ready
in 50-55 days after sowing. Yield is 3.2 -3.8 t/ac.
4. Pusaparvathi:Developed by X ray radiation of American variety. tolerant to
powdery mildew and mosaic. Early type. Pickings can be started 45-55 days after
sowing. Yield 3.2 -3.3 t/ac.
5. Premeir: Early type. Resistant to wilt and mosaic virus. Suitable for Rajma. Yields
around 3.0-3.6 t/ac.
Pole types: T.K.D -1, K.K.L-1. These are long duration of 90-100 days. Yield around
2.0-2.4 t/ac.
Time of sowing: It is a cool loving crop. Sowing can betaken in the months of October –
January. In hills, it is sown during February –March, delayed sowing results in reduced
yields.
Seed rate: 20-24 kg/ac.
Land preparation: 4-5 ploughings are required to get fine tilth. Ridges are made 30-50 cm
apart and seeds are sown at a distance of 25-30 cm on the ridge.
Fertilizers: It has poor nodule formation capability, well decomposed FYM up to a dosage of
8 to 10 t/ a is given, besides that 8 kg N, 20 kg P and K are applied per acre. Nitrogen is
applied in two splits. Half nitrogen first split is given at the time of sowing whole quantity of
P and K. Second split is given at flowering stage.
Intercultural operations:Alachlor @ 800 g or Pendimethalin 1.2 l in 200 l of water as can
be applied as pre-emergent weedicide. Dwarf varieties do not need support. Climbing
varieties need to be supported with bamboo sticks. Single stick is fixed near each plant. The
frame work consists of line of pairs of caves not less than 42 cm apart at ground level.
Earthing up around the base of the plant gives additional support and encourages root growth.
Irrigation: French bean is said to be a drought resistant crop. For better growth and yield
proper supply of moisture is essential. Irrigation is required in the early phases of crop growth
during blooming and pod development period. Irrigation at regular intervals of 7-10 days is
necessary.
Harvesting: Tender pods are harvested for vegetable purpose, pods are ready in 2-3 weeks
after first bloom. Matured pods which are dried are harvested for seed purpose.
Yield: Bush type - 3.6-4 t/a
Pole type – 4.8 -6.0 t/a
Seed production: Minimum isolation distance of 50 m is maintained. Seeds are separated
from the pods when it turns to yellow colour.
Lecture -27
Chilli and Capsicum –cultivation practices
Chilli
Botanical name: Capsicum fruitiscens– Bell pepper
Capsicum annum -Chilli
Family :Solanaceae
Chilli is also called as Pepper. Green chillies are rich in proteins, Ca, Mg, P, K, Cu
and S. vitamins like Thiamine, Riboflavin and Vitamin C. Pungency of chillies is due to
capsaicin. The pigment (colour) in chillies is due to capsanthin also contains many other
oleoresins.
Climate:Chilli is grown in both tropical and sub-tropical areas. It requires warm humid
climatefor vegetative growth while, it requires warm dry weather for fruit maturity. It needs a
well distributed annual rainfall of about 800 – 1200 mm. Heavy rainfall leads to poor fruit set
and high humidity leads to fruit rot. The crops continue to develop at high temperature but
root development is retarded at a temperature of 300 C. Fruit development is adversely
retarded at 380 C. Average night temperature favours high capsaicin content.
Soil:Chilli can be grown on a wide variety of soils provided. For rainfed crop, black soils and
for irrigated crop black soils, chalka soils, sandy loam soils are ideal. Strongly acid soils and
alkaline soils are not suitable.
Land preparation: It needs fine tilth. To bring fine tilth land should be ploughed 3-4 times
followed by 2 harrowings.
Seed rate: Transplanted crop – 650 g per cent
Broadcasting - 2.5 kg per acre.
Seed treatment: At first seeds are treated with 150 g Trisodium orthophosphate to prevent
viruses followed by 8 g Imidachloprid against sucking pest and finally treated with fungicides
like Capton 2 to 3 g per litre used to prevent seed borne diseases.
Nursery management: nursery beds of 4 m length, 1 m width and 15 cm height are
prepared. 30 cm channel is provided in between the beds. Beds are drenched with 1%
Bordeaux mixture or 3 g COC on 9th and 13th day of sowing. Seedlings are ready for
transplanting in 6 weeks.
Varietites:
G-3: long fruited type. Suitable for rainfed crop.
G-4 (Bhagyalaxmi): fruits are long. Used for both green and red chilli purpose. Tolerant to
virus. Yield 40-45 q/acre.
G-5 (Andhrajyothi): fruits are short called gundu types. Yield 40-50 q/acre.
C.A.960 (Sindhur): Fruits alr long and thick. Suitable for green and red chilli purpose under
irrigated crop. Early fruiting with less pungent mainly suitable for summer crop.
L.C.A. -200 (Kiran): Long fruited type. Suitable for Telangana under irrigated conditions+.
Yields 40-45 q /a.
C.A. 1068 (Aparna): fruits are stout and long serves for dual purpose. Yields 35-40 q/ha.
Paprika types: Fruits are long, thick and less pungent and bright coloured. These are used
mainly for pickles, salads and for oleoresin preparations and have good demand in European
markets.
Time of Sowing: Kharif – July to August
Rabi – October to November
Transplanting: Six weeks oldseedlings are suitablefor transplanting. Seedlings are
transplanted at 60 cm x 15 cm for rainfed crop. Under irrigated crop seedlings are
transplanted with a spacing of 60 cm x 60 cm or 75 cm x 60 cm or 90 cm x 60 cm.
Weed management: Fluchloralin 45 % @ 1 litre per acre or pendimethalin 1.3 -1.6 litre or
Oxyflourofin 23.5 % 200 ml any of the above weedicides are sprayed 1 or 2 days prior to
transplanting.
Fertilizers: FYM @ 10 ton per acre is applied at the time of last plough. A fertilizer dose of
60-40-50 kg NPK per ha are applied for rainfed crop and for irrigated crop 300-60-120 kg/ha
NPK are applied.
Harvesting: Fruits are harvested at correct stage of maturity to get maximum yield and dried
on cement floor. 3-4 pickings can be taken from rainfed crop and 6-8 pickings are obtained
from irrigated crop.

Lecture 29
Cultivation of Cucurbits – Cucumber, Pumpkin and Squash
Scientific Name: Cucumis sativum
Family: Cucurbitaceae
Cucumber is used as salad or vegetable. It is rich in vitamin B and C and contains
plenty of water. It also possesses medicinal values. Oil extracted from seeds is good for body
and mind.
Climate:Warm weather is suitable for its cultivation. It cannot tolerate to frost. The condition
of high humidity and short day length will promote female flower production. Cucumber
requires minimum temperature of 180 C for seed germination 200 C for growth and
development.
Soil:Sandy loam soils gives early and good crop. it requires heavy soils will for high yield.
The crop can be grown successfully in slightly acidic soils pH 5.5 to 6.7. The soil should be
with proper drainage facility.
Varieties and hybrids:
Japanese long green: released from IARI. It is an extra early maturing variety. It matures
in 45 days after sowing.
Straight – 8:Released by IARI regional station, Kutrain fruit is light green in colour and
medium size.
PusaSamyog, Solan Hybrid -1 are F1 hybrids: female plants are identified from Japanese
types and planted in separate rows and pollinated naturally with other monoecious plants
thereby the female plants give F1 seeds.
Co-1, Poisettia, PusaKheeraare in cultivation.
Season:Kharif – June-July
Summer – January – March
Seed rate: 1-1.5 kg/ha
Seeds are first treated with Imidachloprid @ 5 g then with Captan /Thiram @ 3 g. per kg.seed
Sowing is done on raised beds or in furrows or in pits. Two seeds per hill are generally sown
in both sides of bed.In case of pit systems pits of 45 x 45 x 60 cm are dug up filled with
FYM, cattle manure and soil in equal proportions 3 to 4 seeds per pit are sown.Spacing
adopted is 1.5 to 3 m from row to row 60 to 90 cm from plant to plant.
Manuring:8 to 10 t per acre of FYM is to be mixed with soil or applied to the pit besides that
about 40 kg N, 20 kg P and 40 kg K per ha need to be applied. Half of Nitrogen, entire P and
K is applied in the pits or at the time of sowing. Remaining quantity of nitrogen is applied at
30 days after sowing.
Irrigation:
Cucumber cannot withstand water logging over irrigation should be avoided in dry weather
crop is irrigated in every 5th day. Flower initiation and full bloom stage are critical. For
irrigation fruit enlargement requires sufficient water.
Inter culture:
Training and pruning: Vines are trained on bamboo with the rope or wire for high
production and quality. Cucumber can be trained in bower system. The height of Bower
should be about 1.5 m and spacing is kept as 2 m x 1 m between row to row and plant to plant
respectively. Japanese long green and hybrids like Pusasamyog are suitable for bower system.
Pruning of secondary shoots up to 10 nodes increase the fruit production. Field
should be kept weed free throughout cropping season. First weeding may be given 15 to 20
days after sowing. Two more weedings are given at 25 to 30 day interval.
Harvesting: Harvesting starts from 45 days after sowing. Fruit takes 7 to10 days from setting
to reach marketable size. Cucumber is harvested when it is till tender and green. Over mature
fruit will fetches less price. Picking can be done at an interval of 2 days yield varies from 80
to 120 Q/ha.
Storage: Fruits are stored at 100C and 85% Relative humidity for 10-14 days. Spots appear
on fruit surface and spoils at low storage temperatures.
Seed extraction: Seeds are extracted by fermentation method and seeds are stored at 6-8%
moisture level.

Cabbage was described as more or less compact leaf formed head. The main stem axil
of the head or true cabbage is sharp and thick. Edible part of cabbage is known as head it is
formed by the development of densely packed leaves around the growing point. Like other
leafy vegetables cabbage is low in proteins, fats, high in fibre which is a good remedy for
constipation. Leaves of cabbage are rich in vitamin A, vitamin C, Phosphorous, Sodium,
Potash and Iron.

Cabbage is one of the important winter vegetables, used in salads, cooked vegetable and
pickled which is called as Sauerkrat.
Climate: Cabbage prefers cool weather and it is mainly cultivated during winter months. it
tolerates frost to a certain extent and a mean temperature of 5-300C is preferred for
production of quality heads. High temperatures reduce the quality of head.
Soil: Sandy loam considered best for an early crop. For late crop heavy soil clay loams and
silty loams are preferred. It can be cultivated luxuriantly in all soil types, except saline soils.
Varieties:Varietiesare grouped according to round, size, shape and colour of leaves. These
are grouped into four types.

quality.
b. Pride of India: Cabbage heads are round and ready for harvest in 60-80 days.
c. Copen hagen market:Heads are round, large and compact.
d. Green express: Heads are large,popular in West Bengal.
2. Flat head or Drum Head group:
a. Pusa Drum Head: It is a selection from EC-6774. It is resistant to Black leg and dry rot
diseases. Late variety takes 100-120 days for harvest.
3. Conical Head group:
a. Jersey wake field: medium duration type ready in 60-80 days.
4. Savoygroup:foliage very much glittered and wrinkled. Leaves are twine with little
bloomy. This group includes chief drum head savoyee.
Example: Drum head savoyee
Sowing Time: Short Duration: August – September
Medium duration: September
Long duration: October
In hills it is sown during March –June for vegetable purpose and for seed production it is
cultivated during July-August.
Seed rate and Spacing: 500 -750 g of seed is required for one hectare. Seeds are mixed with
fine sand and sown in raised beds. 30 -35 days old seedlings of 2-3 leaf stage are transplanted
in main field at a spacing of 60x45-50 cm.
Manures and Fertilizers: 20-25 ton of Farm Yard Manure to be incorporated at the time of
last plough. Superphosphate @150-200 kg, Potash @ 200 kg are to be applied during last
plough. 60-80 kg of Nitrogen is applied in 3 split doses one at 25-30 DAT, 2nd dose at 60
DAT and 3rd dose at 75-80 DAT.
Intercultivation: Earthing up helps to produce healthy heads it is done four to six weeks
after transplanting. Mulching with polyethylene sheet control weed and conserve moisture.
Based on requirement sufficient irrigation regular is required as uneven soil moisture leads to
breaking of heads.
Harvesting: Early varieties mature relatively a high temperature heads become loose at
initial stages bud gradually become harder with cooling temperatures. These are ready to
harvest in about 60-80 days while late varieties take 100-120 days. Heads are harvested when
they attain full size and compact.
Yield:Short duration varieties – 30-35 t/ha
Long duration varieties – 35-40t/ha
Seed yield: 500-600 kg/ha
Storage: Heads are stored at 00C and 85% Relative humidity for few weeks and at room
temperature these can be stored for 4-5 days.
Seed production: Cabbage is highly cross pollinated crop. Minimum isolation distance of
800 m is to follow for seed production. Seed production is mainly employed in hills. Seed
production is done by following methods
1. Head intact method: In this method, head is kept intact and only a cross cut is given
to facilitate the emergence of stalk.
2. Stump intact method: Heads are cut just below the base by means of sharp knife,
keeping the stem with whorl of leaves. Beheaded portion of plant is called stump.
Seed production is high in this method.
3. Core intact method: The outer leaves are removed in all sides with downward
perpendicular cuts in such a way that central core is not damaged.
Cauliflower
Scientific Name: Brassica oleracea var. botrytis
Family: Cruciferae
Cauliflower is a rich source of vitamin A, C, Phosphorous, Calcium, Magnesium, Sodium,
Iron and Carbohydrates. The terminal cluster forms a firm, succulent immature inflorescence
(cluster of flower) is known as curd.
Climate: Cauliflower is a cool weather crop and response well to temperature and
photoperiod.The average optimum monthly temperature is 15-20OC with the average
maximum at 250C and the minimum at 80 C. Early varieties require higher temperature in
short days. At relatively lower temperature the curds of early varieties become ricy, leafy,
loose and yellow resulting in poor quality. In case of late varieties the curds remain under
sized or small, showing some signs of bolting at relatively lower temperature. In hot dry
weather, the curd becomes small and hard.
Soil: Fairly deep loamy soils are preferable even it can be grown in sandy loam, silt loams
and clay loams. Soil should be rich organic matter and well drained.Cauliflower is sensitive
to high acidity.It requires an average pH of 5.5 to 6.6.
Varieties: Cauliflower has specific temperature and photoperiod for its proper growth. Thusit
is very essential that the early, mid and late varieties are planted at proper time. In general
short duration varieties are small, light yellow in colour, medium duration ones are big sized
with white colour curds and long duration varieties are milky white in colour. Based on the
duration varieties are grouped into three types.
Short duration varieties: Suitable for early planting in season. Curds are ready in 70-80
days. Curds are small and yellow in colour.
Eg: PusaKatki, Early Market, Early Kunwari, Pusa Deepali
Medium or Main crop: Suitable for planting in middle of the season. Curds are ready in 90-
100 days. Curds become loose and turns to yellow if delayed in harvesting.
Eg: Snowball, Giant Snowball
Long duration varieties: Suitable for late season planting. takes 100-120 days for
harvesting. Curds are medium in size and milky white.
Eg: Snowball – 16, Pusa Snowball-1
Four types of curds:
1. Ricy:Inflorescence stalk is long, curds are loose and small. It is due to high
temperature at maturity or delay in harvest. Selection of good quality seed and timely
sowing is essential to overcome it.
2. Fizzy: Long stretched stalk with velvety curds. It may be due to genetic character or
unfavorable weather conditions.
3. Leafy Curds: Due to unfavorable growing conditions, small leaves appear in the
middle of curds.
4. Matured curds: Curds attain its full size and colour.
Sowing time:Short duration varieties: July – August
Medium duration varieties: August- September
Long duration varieties: September- October
Seed rate: short duration varieties – 600-700 g/ ha
Long duration varieties – 350-400 g/ha
Seeds are mixed with fine sand and sown in nursery beds. Seedlings of 30-35 days age are
transplanted in the main field.
Spacing: Short duration varieties – 45 x 45 cm
Medium and Long duration varieties – 60 x 45 cm
Fertilizers: Phosphorous and Potassic fertilizers @ 40-50 kg and 50 kg/ha are applied during
last plough. Nitrogenous fertilizers 2 60-80 kg/ha are applied in three split doses first at 25-30
days after transplanting, second at 50-60 DAT and third at 75-80 DAT.
Boron and Molybdenum deficiencies are found when it grown in acidic or basic soils. For
this Boron @ 0.3 -0.4% is sprayed twice one at two weeks after transplanting and before curd
initiation. To overcome Molybdenum deficiency, Sodium Molybdate @ 1-2 kg /ha is applied
in soil.
Intercultivation and Irrigation: Gap filling after 20 days of planting to maintain the
population and uniform growth. Hoeing and weeding on 30th and 45th day is done. Avoid
deep inter cultivation as it is a shallow rooted crop.Irrigation is given once in a week based on
soil moisture availability.
Blanching: Covering of the growing curds withlower leaves is called blanching. It is done to
protect the curds from sunlight with the help of thread or rubber bands. It helps in easier
harvesting if it is done with different coloured threads / bands.
Harvesting: Curds are harvested when they attain full size. Usually curds are harvested along
with 2-3 leaves for easy transport. These can be stored at room temperature for 4-5 days. At a
temperature of 1 0C and Relative Humidity of 85-90% curds can be stored for about 30 days.
Yield:When the cauliflower curds mature at a higher temperature above 250C, the curds are
small, loose and yellow.In spite of closer spacing which is followed by the growers, the yield
hardly exceeds 10 t/ ha.With cooler season, the midseason cultivars can yield upto 20 t/ha.
Physiological disorders in cauliflower:
1. Buttoning
2. Riceyness
3. Browning
4. Whiptail
Buttoning: This disorder is characterized by development of small curd. Buttoning may be
due to overaged seedlings, poor nitrogen supply, planting wrong cultivar, i.e., early cultivar
planted late and also due to root injury by insects or by some disease. It can be overcome by
transplanting 21-25 days old seedlings, application of optimum dose of nitrogenous fertilizers
and transplanting of the early season cultivars in time.
Riceyness: Premature initiation of floral buds is characterized by riceyness in cauliflower and
is considered to be of poor quality for marketing. Such disorder may result from any
temperature higher or lower than the optimum required for a particular cultivar. Choosing the
cultivars which can tolerate high temperature and timely harvesting of the curds can
overcome riceyness.
Browning: This is caused by boron deficiency. It appears as small water soaked areas in the
centre of the curd. Later, the stem becomes hollow with soaked tissue surrounding the walls
of the cavity. In more advanced stage, pinkish or rusty brown areas develop on the surface
of the curd and hence, it is also known as brown rot or red rot. Affected curd develops a
bitter taste. It can be controlled by application of borax or sodium borate @ 20 kg/ha. In
case of acute deficiency, spray of 0.25 to 0.50% solution of borax @ 1 to 2 kg/ha is
advocated.
Whiptail:This results due to deficiency of molybdenum. The leaf blades do not develop
properly and become strap-like. The growing point is severely deformed and no marketable
head is formed. It occurs in acidic soil below pH 4.5. Whiptail can be prevented by brining
the soil pH to 6.5 by liming with 5-7.5 t/ha of limestone or by applying 2.5-5 kg/ha of
sodium or ammonium molybdate. Foliar spray with 0.05% sodium molybdate solution is
also recommended.
Blindness: It is supposed to be due to low temperature when the plants are small or due to
damage to the terminal bud during handling of the plant or due to insect pest like cut worms
which eat the terminal bud.

Cultivation of Carrot – Management practices
Carrot
Scientific Name: Dacus carota
Family: Umbelliferae
Carrot is grown all over India and is used for human consumption as well as forage
and particularly for feeding. It is taken raw as well as cooked in curries and is made into
pickle and sweets.
Black carrots are used for the preparation of a sort of beverage called kanji, which is
a support to be a good appetite.The orange coloured varieties are rich in carotene a precursor
of vitamin A and contain appreciable quantity of thiamine and riboflavin.
For every 100g carrot
Vitamin A - 3.150 mg
Carbohydrates - 10.6 mg
Sodium – 35.6 mg
Potash – 108 mg
Climate: Carrot is cool season crop.Some of the tropical types tolerate quite high
temperature. Colour development and growth of roots is affected by temperature. At the
temperature of 15 to 200 Ccolour development is good.At the temperature of 20- 250 C results
in poor colour development. At high temperatures length of the root is short and at low
temperature root length is long.
Soil: It requires deep well drained sandy loam. This type of soil is particularly good for early
crop. Heavy soils will check the development of roots and cause forked lateral roots.Carrot
does not grow well in highly acidic soil. Maximum yield can be obtained at pH of 6.5.
Types:
They are two groups.
1. Asiatic type
2. European type
1. Asiatic types:These are red in colour due to anthocyanin pigments. Roots are long
and smooth with conical shaped root ends. Produce roots and seeds freely in the
plains.
Ex: Pusa Kesar – a cross between Local Red and Nantes.
2. European types: Roots are small. Roots become hard if delay in harvesting. Rich in
carotene.
Ex:Nantes, Chanteny
Bolting: Production of flowering before the crop is harvested is known as bolting. Bolting
results in poor root growth.
Time of Sowing: September – January
Year round cultivation is possible in areas where the summer temperatures are less.
Seed rate: 5-6 kg/ha.
Method of sowing &Spacing: Seeds are thin and light they are mixed with soil at 1:10 ratio.
Seeds are sown to a depth of 1 to5 cm at a spacing of 30 cm between rows (within rows 5
cm). The seeds germinate within 5 to 10 days after sowing under good moisture conditions.
Thinning has to be done at distance 5 to10 cm. Thinning is done at 8 to 10days after
germination. Optimum spacing is 30 x 5-10 cm.
Manures & Fertilizers: Carrot is a heavy feeder. 20-30 t of farm yard manureis applied at
the time of last plough. Fresh Cowdung should not be applied it may cause forking of roots.
Fertilizer dose of 60 kg Nitrogen, 50 kg Phosphorous and 100 kg Potash to be appliedbefore
sowing.
Irrigation:First irrigation is given soon after seed sowing this has to be followed. Four to six
days after sowing. Irrigation is given at 6 to 10 days interval.
Earthing up: Should be done at 60 to 70 days after sowing to help in development of roots.
The soil is earthed up covered the top of developing roots to prevent loss of colour of tops,
the tops becomes green and toxic on exposure to sun light.
Harvesting: Early carrots are harvested when they are partly developed.For the purpose of
distinct markets otherwise they are retained in the soil till they reach full maturity stage they
should not be retained afterward.There are two methods of harvesting.
1. Roots are dug out when they are sufficiently moist withkhurpi or spade. Light
irrigation has to be given before harvest, so that easy pulling of roots can be facilitated
without damage by holding the leaves.
In case of Asiatic variety the roots are harvested when they attain marketable stage 2.5 to
5 cm in diameter, at the upper end after harvesting the roots they are trimmed and washed
before sending them to the market.
Yield: Tropical types give around 20 to 30 ton per ha.
Storage: At 00C -4.5 0C and 98% RH carrots are stored for 3-5 months.
Seed production:
a. In-situ Method:Plants with matured roots are left in the field for flowering. Seeds
produced in this method are of poor quality.
b. Transplanted method: After development of the roots selected plants are transplanted in
other place. Seeds produced in this method are of good quality. Seeds yield of 5-6 q/ ha can
be obtained in this method.

Cultivation of Onion – Management practices
Scientific name: Allium cepa
Family:Amarylladaceae
It is consumed either raw or cooked along with spices and vegetables. Primarly the
bulbs used as vegetables. The flowering shoot known as Scape is also used as vegetable.It is
rich in minerals like phosphorus and calcium and carbohydrates.It also contains Protein and
Vitamin C.
Pungency in onion is due to the presence of a volatile compound called “Allyl Propyl
di Sulphide”. Red colour is due the pigment anthocyanin and yellow colour is due to
Quercetin.
Climate: Onion is best suited as a tropical crop. It does best where the season is mild without
the extremes of heat or cold or excessive rainfall. A relatively high temperature as well as
long photo period (a temperature of 15.6 to 21.1O C for about 10 hours a day and about 80%
RH) is essential for bulb formation.
Soil: It grows best in light soils which may be sandy loam or silt loam. Sandy soils with high
organic matter are suitable. It is sensitive to higher acidity and the optimum pH of the soil
should range from 5.8 to 6.5 and the land should be prepared to fine tilth. Soils with poor
drainage, saline soils are not suitable.
Varieties: Onion varieties are red, white and yellow in colour.
Red coloured varieties: N-53, Pusa Red, Nasik Red, Hissar -2, Punjab Selection
White coloured varieties: Pusa white flat, Pusa white round, Punjab -48, Udaipur -102
Yellow coloured varieties: Early Grano, Bermuda Yellow, ArkaPitambar (Less pungent one
suitable for export purpose to Europe countries).
Hybrids: ArkaLalima: suitable for export purpose to Gulf countries.Resistant to leaf spot
disease and can be stored for 5 months.
ArkaKeertiman: Red coloured variety suitable for both Kharif and Rabi seasons. Suitable
for export purpose.
Season Time of Sowing Time of Transplanting
Kharif June –July First fortnight of August
Rabi October – January First fortnight of December
Seed rate: 3-4kg of seed is sufficient to transplant seedlings for one acre. Seeds are sown in
raised beds of 4 m length, 1 m width and 15 cm height. 6 to 8 weeks old seedlings which are
about 15 cm tall are transplanted.Fordirect sowing the seed rate has to be doubled.
Bulbs:When bulbs are planted the seed rate is 1000 to 1200 per Ha.Bulbs of about 1/2inch
diameter are dibbled on one side of ridge or in plain beds.
Spacing: 20 x10 cm2 for seedlings, 30 x10cm2 for bulbs. Seeds are treated with Captan or
Thiram (3g/kg seed) or Trichidermaviridae (4 g/kg). Drenching with Copper Oxy Chloride
@ 3g/ l is done at 10 days interval to avoid damping off disease.
Carbofuran 3 G granules @ 100 g are applied in mixing with fine sand.
Manuring: 25 ton of FYM,60 to 100 KgN, 40 to 60 Kg P O and 60 to 80 Kg ofK O. FYM
2 5 2
should be incorporated at the time of field preparation, P and K along with half of N should
be applied in bands, 5 cm below the seedlings to the side before transplanting. The rest of N
may be top dressed 2 months after planting.
Irrigation: It requires 14-18 irrigations from planting to harvest depending on the season. At
bulb formation stage i.e 70 to 75 days after planting irrigation is essential.Drought at this
stage results in cracking of the bulb and low yield.
Harvesting: Green bunch onions areharvested when they are lead pencil thickness with a
small bulb, as a direct vegetable.
As a bulb crop is comes to harvest after four months of planting. A well matured bulb
should be harvested by putting out or digging out the bulbs.Maturity is indicated by the tops
dropping just above the bulb while the leaves are still green. The outer scales on the bulbs
become loose and coloured.
Yield:Kharif- 80-100 t/ac
Rabi – 120-140 t/ac
Storage:After harvesting onions are dried under shade. Application of Maleic Hydrazide
@2000 ppm before 15 days of harvesting improves the storage life by 8 months.
Precautions to be taken:
• Withheld of irrigation before 15 days of harvesting.
• Bulbs should be shade dried.
• The bulb after harvesting are left in the field under shade for four days for curing
which helps the bulbs in improvement of colour and quality of bulbs.
Physiological disorders: The phenomenon ofpremature production of seed stalk is known as
bolting. It reduces the growth of the bulbs. Some of the salient features of bolting are the
bolts are little bit smaller in size than normal inflorescence. Bolting occurred to the extent of
50 to 80% in the onions planted in the later part of kharif or early rabi season. Bolting may be
due to one or two more factors like varietal difference, extremes of temperature, growth
obstacles, poor seed quality, poor soil, amount of sun shine etc.
Seed production: Seed production is possible in tropical plains. Onion is a Cross pollinated
crop hence an isolation distance of 1000 m to be maintained.There are two methods in seed
production.
Bulb to seed method: In this method, bulbs of 2.5 – 3 cm diameter are required @ 1500
kg/ha for seed production. Bulbs are planted during first fortnight of October in beds or
ridges at a spacing of 45 x 15 cm. flowering commences 3 months after planting thereby seed
formation takes within 1-11/2 months and are ready for harvest. To prevent the loss of seed
from burst heads should harvest when it matures without delay. Seed should be dried for 1-2
days in shade. This method is used for nucleus and foundation seed production. Seed yield of
8010 q/ha which is less as compared to seed to seed method.
Seed to seed method: Seeds are sown in nursery beds from September - November and
transplanted in November – December. Bulbs are ready in April-May. Good quality bulbs are
selected and these are again planted in the months of September – October. Seed formation
will be completed by April –May. It takes around 11/2 year for seed production with seed
yield of 10-15 q/ha. This method is useful in varieties which are not suitable for storage or to
produce seed in huge quantity of a new variety.

Cultivation of Colacasia and Elephant foot yam
Colacasia
Scientific name: Colacasia esculenta
Family:Areace
Colacasia is a minor tuber crop, mainly cultivated for edible roots.Tubers of colacasia are
called as corms and these are used for making chips. Leaves and young leaf stalks are also
cooked as used as spinach. Corms and cormels, petioles and leaves we used as vegetable.
Tubers have allergic reaction due to the presence of calcium oxalate.
Climate:High temperature with high humidity is congenial for its successful cultivation.
Soil:In tropical areas, it requires frequent irrigation and hence soils with high water holding
capacity are good to take up the cultivation of Colocasia.Colocasia is grown in heavy soils
and can withstand to some extent water logged conditions.
Varieties:
1. KovvurShathamukhi: Released from APAU. Tubers possess less oxalate. very good
cooking quality. Yields 15 – 20 tonnes per hectare.
2. Kasi Bugga: Tuber yield of 12-15 t/ha.
3. Panchamukhi: Mainly used as leafy vegetable. Tubers yield of 23 t/ha.
Season: In our state, crop can be cultivated from February to April while in coastal districts
of Andhra Pradesh it is cultivated twice i.e. June- July and Feb- Apr.
Seed rate and Spacing:Cormels or daughter corms in some cases mother corms also used for
planting material. Large size cormels are better than the mother corms.The plant material is
stored in a shady place and covered with leaves. The cormels are pre-sprouted and healthy
corms are selected for planting. around one tonne seed / corms are required for one hectare.
Spacing: 60 x 20 cm.
Intercultivation:Regular weeding is done to keep the field as weed free. Mulching is
practices with dry lands per plant material that given organic matter.
Manuring: Well decomposed FYM @ 12.5 to per ha along with 60, 60 and 60 kg of N, P, K
per hectare are applied. Irrigation throughout the life period is beneficial when rainfed
cultivation is adopted.Increase in the number of supplementary irrigations should increase
yield.
Harvesting: It takes 3 months formaturity is indicated by yellowing of leaves later on turns
to brown colour. Tubers are harvested by digging with pick axe.
Yield: 15-25 t/ ha.
Storage: Daughter corms are separated from mother corms and cleaned by removing the
adhering soil. These can be stored for 2-21/2 months without sprouting.
Elephant Foot Yam
Scientific name:Amarphophaluscompanulatus
Family:Araceae
It is cultivated in tropical and subtropical areas.
Climate: Climatic requirement of yam depends on different stages of growth. For vegetative
growth well distributed rainfall with warm and humid and for tuber development cool and dry
climate is essential. Heavy rains and water stagnating conditions cause tuber rot.
Soil: it can be grown from light to heavy soils though a rich red-loamy soil with a pH range
of 5.5 -7.0 is preferred.
Varieties: Gajendra and Sree Padma are the popular varieties.
Time of sowing: February – April
Seed rate and Spacing: Propagation is by tubers and are used after 2-21/2 months after
harvest. Tubers of ½ -3/4 kg are used. If tubers are large, they are cut into 2-4 pieces and
should possess a sprouting bud. Tubers are planted at a spacing of 90 x 90 cm and a depth of
10-15 cm.
Manures and Fertilizers: well decomposed Farm Yard Manure @ 25-30 t/ha, NPK @ 150 –
50-150 kg/ha. Entire P should be applied during last plough. Nitrogen and Potash fertilizers
are applied in 3 split doses at 45, 90 and 120 days after planting.
Intercultivation: Need based weeding and irrigation is to be given.
Harvesting: tubers are ready in 8-10 months after planting and are harvested by digging with
pick axe. Harvested tubers are cleaned and shade dried for 1-2 months.
Yield: 60-70 t/ha.

Flowers are being used for various social and religious offerings in all the cultures.
Cultivation of flowers both as cut flower and loose flower purpose are gaining importance
due to the increase in standard of living. Considering the horticulture industry, flower

addition to earn foreign exchange. Different segments like cut flower cultivation, loose

material production, colour pigments, dried flowers, perfumes and essential oil production are
provides enormous scope in floriculture. According to the estimates done during 2018-19,

Garden Features:
Ornamental gardens are meant for beauty and recreation purpose. In laying of any garden, use
of various garden components breaks the monotony and enhances the aesthetic value. Some
of the garden features are as:
Lawn: it is one of the most important components of a garden gives a view of green carpet
on the ground. It not only enhances the beauty and makes the area to look large.
Hedge: shrubs or trees planted at regular intervals to form a continuous screen is called a
hedge. It serves the purpose of screening of unwanted places. These are pruned to maintain a
height of 50 to 60 cm.

Edge: Lining of borders of flower beds, paths, lawn and shrubbery with brick, concrete,
living plants etc ., is known as edge. The main purpose of edge is demarcation or decoration.
Plants with dwarf growth and which withstands frequent trimming are used for edging.
Plants used : Alternanthera, Eupatorium.
Rockery: this is intended to bring together in a short space an idea of a mountain or garden
with plants growing in the crevices of rocks. This is an elevated structure resembling a
miniature mountain range or slope of a hill with a few dominant peaks.
Fence:fence is a utility item essentially needed for marking the boundary and for protection
and also put to separate one part of the garden from the other. Several materials such as
wood, bamboo, wire, wire nettings are used for fence.
Drives, roads, walks and Path:all these in a garden should be laid out after due
consideration is given to its necessary and artistic appeal.They should serve to link one part
with the other part. Paths may be made up of earth, brick and concrete or be paved.

which are amenable for bending and withstand frequent trimming are suitable for developing
topiary.

Lecture 35
Ornamental gardens – formal gardens – informal gardens - features
An ornamental garden is a place where plants are arranged in an aesthetic manner.
Plants can be grouped together in various ways to give an aesthetic effect. Each such
grouping is called a Feature. Any garden comprises some of all of such features and hence
the features are also called the components of garden.
Styles of garden: two types of styles garden
5. Formal gardens
6. Informal gardens
1.Formal garden: in this type of gardens, everything is done in as straight and narrow way in
a symmetrical or a geometrical pattern. Everything is planted in straight lines. The hedges,
edges and topiary are maintained in proper shape by regular training and pruning. Symmetry
is always maintained in the garden by undertaking similar type of plantation and using similar
garden technique and adornments. If there is one type of plants or featureson the one side of
garden, the same thing should also be repeated on the other side of the garden.
Eg: Mughal garden, French garden
1. Mughal gardens: These gardens are laid during the Mughal’s period and Babar (1494 -
1531) was the first emperor to introduce Mughal gardens into India. These are the replica of
gardens Central Asia, Persia.
Features of Mughal Gardens:
1. Site and Design: Mughals always selected site on hill slope with perennial source of
water or along with the banks of perennial river. The gardens were mostly square or
rectangular in the shape.
2. Walls and Gates: These gardens were surrounded with high walls so that it may not be
easily accessed by enemies and protection from hot winds. The entrance was provided with
huge wooden gates studded with iron nails and pointed iron spikes.
3.Terraces: Mughals came from hilly terrain. So they had intrinsic inclination towards
terrace.Some gardens have seven terraces corresponding to seven planets.
4. Tomb or Mosque: It was common practice to create garden around Tomb or Mosque.
Usually, Mughal gardens have been developed with a monument of Tomb or Mosque.
Ex: Taj garden around Taj mahal.
5. Baradari: This feature with permanent roof and raised platform for sitting. Baradari
usually provided with 12 doors on all sides. These were constructed to enable the emperor to
watch the performance of dancing, rain shower.
2.French Gardens: During 16th century, these styles of gardens gained importance with the
contribution of Le-Notre (1643-1700 A.D.) at Vaux-Le-Vicomte. The French garden style
seems to teach the lesson of “How to think Big”.
3. Informal Gardens: Informal gardens are laid not in a definite pattern. These are laid to
imitate the nature. Roads, paths are not laid in a definite design. Trees, other plants are grown
particularly for their colour and not according to their height.
Ex: Japanese gardens, English gardens
1. English gardens:Due to favourable climatic conditions, such as high annual rainfall, the
natural ground cover in the England is grass. In consonance to this, the famous British
architect Repton and Brown advocated the concept that the British garden which look like
the country side without any artificial barriers such as fences or hedges, etc.
The main features of the garden:
a) curved paths
b) informal group of trees
c) lawn
d) herbaceous border
e) shrubbery and rockery
2.Japanese Gardens:An open space, a pond with an island in the midst of it, hillock on the
south of pond and a stream of water consisted typical feature of garden. Water stream is
divided into two parts, one is directed to pond and the other one is directed to hillock to have
a water fall. Immutability is another strong feature of Japanese gardens. Except some
seasonal changes in the deciduous trees, the Japanese garden hardly goes under any other
strong visible changes during different season. Even during winter, the Japanese garden has
their own beauty with snowflakes hanging down the stone pieces or stone lanterns.

Rose is top most cut flower crops cultivated globally and considered as queen of flowers.
There are different classes of roses as
