4. Climbing Roses: These climb against a support and produces small flowers in flushes.
Ex: Climbing summer snow, climbing snowball
5. Damask: Suitable for oil extraction due to their fragrance.
6. Grandifloras: Produces large flowers in bushes. Suitable for growing in gardens and
for loose flowers also.
Soil: Roses can be successfully grown in red loam, sandy loam and silty loam soils. Soil pH
of 6.5 – 7.5 is ideal for rose but sensitive to saline soils. Soils rich in organic matter with
good water holding capacity are ideal for its cultivation.
Climate: Rose is a sun loving plant which needs at least 8 hours of sunlight. Temperature
fluctuations affect flower yield and quality adversely. Day and night temperatures of 300C
and 150C are ideal whereas, colour development takes place at 180C.
Propagation: Rose is propagated by means of stem cuttings and budding. It is commercially
propagated by T-budding. Rosa indica and Rosa multiflora are suitable for root stock
purpose.
Spacing: Depending upon the soil types, roses are planted at a spacing of 75-120 cm. Pits of
45 cm X 45 cm X 30 cm size are prepared for plantation of rose plantlets. Pits are exposed
to sun for about 15 days then the pits are refilled with soil –manure mixture. Commercially
grown hybrids are planted at a spacing of 60 x 60 cm which accommodates 8500 plants per
acre.
Planting time:though it can be planted from June – January, the best time for planting roses
is during September – October.
Irrigation: light watering is given after planting to till new growth appears, thereafter
irrigate the plants at 8-10 days interval.
Pruning:Pruning is done to produce best quality flowers and to maintain good shape and to
keep plants healthy by removing dead parts. Three to four months after planting the rose
plant is first pruned. Four branches placed in four directions are chosen and these are pruned
back to an outer bud leaving two to four buds on the stump. Pruning is done once in a year
during October- November months. Hybrid Teas are pruned 45 days before and Floribundas
are pruned 42 days before flowering.
1. All the dead, dried, weak branches are to be pruned.
2. Any new growth appear on the root stock should be removed regularly.
3. Strong shoots are pruned to desired height (depends on the type) with a sharp knife at least
5 mm above the outer side of the bud.
4. Centre of the plant should be pruned to penetrate light, air which improves the flower size.
5. In Tea roses strong shoots are pruned to 2/3 of their length whereas in of Floribundas are
pruned to 1/4 of their length.
6. Bordeaux paste is applied at the pruned surfaces.
Fertilizers: Immediately after pruning, each plant should be nourished with 7-8 kg of FYM,
3-5 kg of Neem cake. 15-20 days after this, Urea, Phosphorous and Potash should be mixed
in 1:8:3 ratios and 100 g of these mixture is to apply for each plant and it is applied for 2-3
times. In addition, micronutrients viz., MgSo @ 20 g, MnSo @ 15 g, Feso @ 10 g, Borax
4 4 4
@ 5 g should be mixed in one litre of water and sprayed before flowering to increase flower
size.
Yield: After initial planting in July- August, Rose starts blooming from October and plant
will yield on economic scale for 3 years.For commercial purpose, Roses areplucked at the
bud stage.
Plant Protection:
Pests:
1. Beetles: these eat the leaves during night time. This can be managed by applying 15 kg of
Malathion 5% dust at evening times.
2.Thrips: These are very minute insects which distort the leaves. Curled leaves with brown
marks and deformed buds with burnt margins are the main symptoms of damage. Spraying of
Fipronil 2ml/l or Profenofos 2ml/l or Imidacloprid at 0.3 ml/l reduces the infestation.
3. Red Spider Mite: Very minute insects or mites spin webs on the underside of leaves. Red
mites infest only during dry months. The affected leaves look dull as mite suck sap from
leaves. Insecticidal spray with Dicofol, and dusting with Sulphur can control this pest.
Diseases:
1.Powdery mildew: Foliage, young stems and stalk of flower buds of rose are coated with
powdery dust. Affected petals lost its colour and wither and dry.
Control: Spraying with Dinocap 1ml or Carbendazim 1 g per litre of water reduces the
infestation.
2. Black spot: circular black spots on the leaves causing severe defoliation and is a common
fungal disease of rose. Initially, brown or yellow spots appear on the lower leaves which then
turn into black spots. The affected leaves turn yellow and fall off. In severe cases leaves drop
and growth ceases.
Control: Spraying of Captan 2 g or Mancozeb 2 g or Carbendazim 1 g per litre of water.
3. Die-Back: This is the most dreaded disease of rose. The stems die back from top down
wards and gradually the whole plant. Stem and roots turns to brown colour.
Control:The affected stem or branch is cut 2-3 inches below the effected part and a cap of
fresh cow-dung mixed with Copper Sulphate or Bordeaux paste alone is put over the cut
wound.
Rose based products – Perfume and allied products
1. Rose oil or Rose perfume:It is obtained from rose petals which possess sweet fragrance,
medicinal properties and used in Ayurvedaas ant bactericide. Bulgarian rose otto is largely
used in perfuming soaps & cosmetics. Used in flavoring soft drinks and alcoholic liqueurs.
Species suitable: Rosa demascena, R. borboniana, R. centifolia, R. alba&R. gallica.
In India,R. demascena and R. borboniana are cultivated for rose oil.
2. Rose water: it is also prepared from petals of rose. Used for fragrance, medicine and
confectionary. Rose water is also used to cool the body, eye lotions, eye drops for its soothing
qualities and also used in drinking water. It is sprinkled on guests at weddings, feasts and
other social functions.
Species which are used for oil/perfume preparation is also suitable for rose water.
3. Gulkand: Rose petals are also preserved for direct consumption prepared by beating equal
proportion of petals and sugar.It is considered as good tonic and laxative.
Species suitable: R. damascene, R. chinensis, R. gallica
4. Pankhuri:Dried Rose petals are known as Pankhuri. They are occasionally used for
preparing sweetened cold drinks.
5. Gul-roghan: Rose petals are mixed with wet sesame seeds to prepare hair oil which is
known as Gul-roghan.
6. Rose syrup: Rose fruits are called as hips from which syrup is prepared. Rose hips are rich
in vitamin C (150 mg/100 g) which is 3 times higher than orange.
Species suitable: Rosa rugosa, Rosa glauca
Other products like Rose vinegar, rose petal wine, Jam, Jelly are prepared in Europe
countries.
Lecture 37
Jasmine - Species – Management practices
Scientific Name: (Jasminum sps.)
Family: Oleaceae
Jasmine is one of the important flower crops grown on commercial scale in
Rangareddy, Nalgonda, Mahabubnagar and Medak districts. The flowers are highly fragrant
and used for religious offerings and also used for preparing garlands. Loose flowers are also
used for extraction of essential oil which is used in the preparation of perfumes and scented.
Soil and Climate:Jasmine can be planted on a wide range of soils. Well-drained sandy loams
and red loams are ideal for its cultivation. In clayey soils, there is increased vegetative growth
and reduced flowering. They give good yield in low rainfall conditions. It is a tropical crop
and grows well in moderate humid conditions.
Varieties
Three species are commercially cultivated in Telangana
i)Jasminum sambac(Gundu malle/ Arabian jasminum/ Tuscan jasmine):Its flower buds are
white with single or multi whorled petals and Jasminum sambac is usually cultivated on
commercial jasmine. Important varieties are Gundumalle, Ramanadhapuram, Motia,
Virupakshi, Sujimalli, Madanabanam, Ramabanam.
ii)Jasminum auriculatum:Commonly known as ‘kakada’, The plants produce numerous star
shaped long flowers, white scented blooms are very good as loose flowers. The flowers are
commonly used for garlands, adorning hair, worship and decoration. It bears flowers from
spring to summer and in rainy season. Common varieties are.Co-1 Mullai,Co-2 Mullai,Long
Round,Short Point,Short Round.
iii) Jasminum grandiflorum:It produces fragrant flowers and flowers have a reddish tinge of
sepals and suitable for loose flowers and oil extraction. The flowers bloom during November
to February.
Propagation:Jasmine species are propagated by cuttings and layers.The rooting of cuttings
can be enhanced by using any of the rooting hormones like IBA (5000 ppm), IAA (1000
ppm) and NAA (5000 ppm). Simple and compound layering methods are followed during
June – July to October – November. Layers will be ready for planting within 90-120 days.
Planting:After ploughing the land, pits of about 40 x 40 x 40 cm size are dugout and filled
with topsoil and filled with 15 kg of well-rotten FYM.Planting distance depends on the
species and also on soil and environmental conditions.
Species Planting distance
J.sambac 1.2 x 1.2 m
J.auriculatum 1.8 x 1.8 m
J.multiflorum 1.5x 1.5 m
Planting is usually done during June – August.
Irrigation: Irrigation is most important factor for jasmines especially after pruning. Constant
and adequate water supply (irrigating twice a week) in light soils during peak flowering
season (March –October) is essential for high yield of flowers. After flowering is over, the
water supply can be cut off
Manures and Fertilizers:The plants are usually manured once in every year with organic
manures in January before flush season commences at 10-12 kg of FYM, 60-120 g N, 120 g
P O K Oper plant. The manures are usually applied after pruning the bushes once in June-
2 5& 2
July and again December-January.
Pruning: Flowers commences from tender shoots.With the approaching of winter the bushes
start to shed the leaves. To promote good flowering water is withheld in the 2nd fortnight of
November and allow plant to rest and shed the leaves or the plants are defoliated manually.In
Telangana the sheep herd is allowed to graze the leaves instead of manual defoliation which
not only saves labour costs but also improves the soil fertility by sheep castings.
Generally, pruning is done after 2 years of its planting and followed in the month of
December to January in Jasminum by removing all branches upto 45 to 50 cm from ground
level and roots should be exposed for few days. Before pruning irrigation is to be withheld
and all the dried and diseased twigs are to be removed. After pruning, the leaves are also to
be removed and irrigated lightly till flower buds appear. Profusely watering is done at regular
intervals after the appearance of flowers. Pruning time varies with the species as follows:
Species Time of pruning
Jasminum sambac February –March
Jasminum auriculatum
Jasminum multiflorum August –September
Harvest
The plants (layers) starts flowering from 2nd year after planting and the commercial yields
commence from third year onwards. The Jasminum sambac varieties flower profusely in
summer and also in rainy season (i.e. March-August) while Jasminum auriculatum flowers in
June-August, while Jasminum mutiflorum flowers during November to February.
Yield
Yield of flowers and jasmine oil vary according to the species and management practices.
Species Flower Yield (t/ac)
J.sambac 1.0-2.0
J.auriculatum 1.8-3.6
J.mutiflorum 1-2
Since the jasmine flowers are highly perishable and have to be disposed off in the market
within few hours after picking.
Lecture 38
Chrysanthemum – varieties – Management practices
Scientific Name: Chrysanthemum morifoliumRamat.
Family: Compositae
Chrysanthemum is one of the leading flowercrop mainly cultivated for its loose
flowers and recently it is gaining importance for its cut flower cultivation too.
Soil and Climate: Well drained, sandy loam soil with pH of 6.5-7.0 is ideal. It is highly
sensitive to waterlogged conditions. Chrysanthemum is a short day plant and for vegetative
growth it requires long day conditions with bright sunlight and high temperatures ranging
from 20 to 270C. It requires short day and low temperatures ranging from 10 to 270C for bud
formation and flowering.
Flower Types:Chrysanthemum flowers are classified by the kind and arrangement of florets
into five broad groups 1) Singles, 2) Anemones, 3) Pompons, 4) Decorative, 5) Large
flowered.
Varieties: All the cultivated types can be broadly classified into three groups.
1. The small flower type known as Nakshatra Chamanti or Kasturi Chamanthi
2. Medium flower types or PatnamChamanti and
3. Large flower types which are mostly used for flower decorations and for cut flowers.
Among these three types, there are variations in colour ranging between yellow to red
with different shades of admixture.In chrysanthemum, a number of hybrids, promising
varieties and locals are available for commercial cultivation.
The following varieties are suitable for loose flowers in Telangana state are
Yellow Basanthi, Punjab Anuradha, CO-1, Co-3, Yellow Gold, Silper, Raichur
White Ratlam selection, IIHR-13, IIHR-6, Baggi, Mother Theresa, PAU-107
Red Red stone , Red gold, Indira, Co-2
Small Button chrysanthemum
Popular local commercially cultivars are Sugandha white, Sugandha yellow,Marigold
,chandamama yellow, chanadamama white and violet types.
Propagation:Chrysanthemum is commercially propagated by terminal cuttings.Propagation
through suckers is discouraged since there will be transmission of viral diseases from parent
material and also there is no uniform flowering.
Terminal cuttings:The best time of raising nursey is May-June. Select terminal cuttings of
5-7 cm length from healthy stock plants. Dipthe terminal cuttings in 2500 ppm Indole butyric
acid (IBA) or any commercial formulations of rooting hormone and planted in raised nursery
beds or portrays for rooting. Drench the beds or trays with Bavistin @1g/l and spray Aliette
@1g/l to avoid soil borne diseases.The plants are ready for planting in 30-40days.
Planting Season:Chrysanthemum is a short day plant and flowers during cool season.The
best time for planting is June- July while, late varieties can be planted till August.However,
farmers plant in the month of 2nd fortnight of May so as to coincide flowering with festive
season.Flowering starts from September and continues till January.
Planting:Well rooted cuttings are planted in ridges at a spacing of 30 x 30 cm and 44,000
rooted terminal cuttings are required per acre.
Preparation of Land:Land is ploughed 3 to 4 times in March-April and 10 t/acre of
farmyard manure(FYM)is applied in the last ploughand the land is made into beds of
convenient size.
Manures and Fertilizers:During last plough, 10 t of FYM along with the recommended
fertilizers will be applied for one acre(60-80 kg of nitrogen, 32-40 kg P 0 and 60-80 kg K 0
2 2
which are to be applied as basal dose). At the time of first pinching Top dress the crop with
30 kg Nitrogen /acre. Foliar spray of ZnSO 0.25% + MgSO 0.5% is recommended.
4 4
Irrigation and Intercultivation: Irrigate the crop twice a week in the first month and
subsequently at weekly intervals. Irrigation depends on soil and weather conditions. Weeding
and hoeings’s generally done manually as and when required, normally 8-10 times. Mulching
can be takenup on raised bed under drip irrigation system. This not only avoids weeds but
also conserves the moisture.
Horticultural Practices:
i)Staking Staking is necessary for tall growing varieties.
ii)Pinchingis the removal ofterminal buds at 4weeks after planting to induce more side
shoots.This may be repeated on lateral shoots after 7weeks of planting.
iii)Desuckering: Remove the side suckers periodically.
Growth regulators application: Foliar Spray of GA @ 100-150 ppm gives flowers early by

periodically.
Growth regulators application: Foliar Spray of GA @ 100-150 ppm gives flowers early by

15-20 and increases the number of blooms per plant, while application of 100 ppm NAA
before flower bud initiation delays blooming.
Harvesting: Depending on the variety, plants start yielding flowers after 3-4 months of
transplanting. The harvesting of the crop commences from September -January and lasts upto
February-March depending upon the time of planting. Fully opened flowers are to be plucked
by hand picking at 4 days interval with or without pedicel (stalk) for loose flowers purpose.
10-15 pickings can be taken up in a season.
Yield: 5-8 tons per acre of loose flowers.
After harvesting of the flowers, the plant is headed back to ground level. Application
FYM and SSP and well irrigation gives raise to suckers, these can be separated and planted.
Other practice is to taking terminal cuttings before removal of crop and placed in nursery.
Before placing it, dipping of the cuttings in 1 g carbendizum should be done. For better
rooting, cuttings are dipped in a hormonal solution of IBA 2500 ppm before planting in
nursery.
Lecture 39
Cultivation of Marigold and Crossandra – Management practices
Scientific name: Tagetes sp.
Family: Compositae
Marigold is one of the most important flowering annuals cultivated round the year. In
recent decades, its cultivation is gaining importance due to some advantages like easy culture
and wide adaptability, wide range of attractive colours, shape, size and good keeping quality.
Soil: It can be grown in a wide range of soils except water logged conditions. However, a
deep fertile soil having good water holding capacity, well drained, sandy loam soil rich in
organic matter is best suitable. Neither too acidic not too alkaline soil with pH 6.0 to 7.5 are
ideal.
Climate: Marigold requires mild climate for luxuriant growth and flowering. Depending on
environmental condition, planting of marigold is done in 3 three season’si.e rainy, summer
and winter. Staggered planting between 1st week of July to 1st week of February at monthly
intervals assures supply of flowers to market over an extended period from October to April,
while, maximum yield can be obtained from September planted crop.
Selection of site: A sunny location is ideal for marigold cultivation. Under shade, it produces
more vegetative growth and do not produce any flowers.
Types:
1. African marigold (Tagetes erecta): Plant height is tall with strong stem. Petals range
from single to multi with large sized flowers. Flowers are available in different shades of
lemon yellow – yellow, golden yellow to orange.
Varieties: Giant Double Yellow, Giant Double Orange, Arka Bangara-1, Arka Bangara-
2, Arka Agni,PusaNarangiGainda.
2. Frenchmarigold (Tagetes patula): it is a dwarf type and grows bushy. Petals range from
single to multi with small sized flowers.Flowers are available in yellow – orange, wheatish
red and a mixture of red, gold and yellow.
Varieties:PusaBasantiGainda, MDU -1.
Seed rate and sowing: 800-1000 g seed is required to plant one acre. Raised beds are
prepared with a dimension of 1 m width and convenient length. Before sowing, Folidol
powder to be applied to protect the seeds from ants. It takes 5-7 days for germination.
Season:
Season Sowing time Trasplanting time
Rainy End of June to 1st week of July First fortnight of august
Winter Mid of September Mid of October
Summer First week of January First week of February
Highest yields are obtained when planted in September. Rainfall during rainy season
and high temperatures during summer will affect the flower quality.
Propagation: Marigold is propagated through seed or herbaceous cuttings. Some varieties do
not set the seed where, cuttings are used for multiplication. Apical shoots of 10cm long are
usually used for vegetative propagation. Herbaceous cuttings each with one or two pair of
leaves are inserted in sand medium either in seed pan or nursery bed.Before putting the
cuttings in rooting medium the basal portion of the cuttings is treated with a hormone powder
which is marketed as Rootex-1 to encourage profuse and early rooting. Shade should be
provided initially to the beds. Regular watering should be done to keep the bed in moist
conditions. Within 8-10 days, rooting is observed in the cuttings which are later used as
planting materials.
Seed: Seeds can be sown on nursery beds in lines in shallow furrows. During preparation of
nursery beds 8-10 Kg of well decomposed FYM per sq.m bed is thoroughly mixed with the
soil. The width of the seed bed should not be more than 1.2m and height should be 15 cm.
Before sowing of seeds a little amount of folidol dust is applied to the nursery bed to avoid
ant or termite infestation. Seeds germinate 5-7 days after sowing.
Transplanting: Land should be ploughed 2 to 3 times to bring the soil to a fine tilth. One
month old seedlings with 3-4 leaves are fit for transplanting. Watering of nursery bed one day
prior to uprooting will lessen the damage to root system. Uprooting of seedlings and
transplanting should be done in the evening hours for better establishment.
Spacing: Seed Cuttings
1) African marigold 45 x 30cm 30 x 20 cm
2) French marigold 20 x 20cm 20 x 10 cm
Manures and Fertilizers: Incorporate 20 ton of Farm Yard Manure during the last plough.
Apply 20-40 kg N, 80 kg of P O and 80 kg of K O per acre. Half of nitrogen, entire dose of
2 5 2
phosphorus and potash should be applied as basal dose, preferably one week after
transplanting and rest half of nitrogen should be applied one month after the first application.
Irrigate after application.
Intercultural operations:Hoeing and weeding should be done 3 to 4 times during the crop
period to make the soil loose and weed free.
Irrigation:At all stages of vegetative growth (55-60 days) and during flower production
sufficient amount of moisture in the soil is essential. Moisture stress at any stage affects
normal growth and flowering.
Pinching: In tall cultivars of African marigold, plants first grow upwards to their final height
and later on produce a terminal flower. After the formation of terminal flower bud, axillary
branches develop which also bear flower. However, if the apical portion of shoot is removed
early, large number of axillary shoots arises resulting in well-shaped bushy plant bearing
more number of uniform sized flowers. Removal of apical portion of shoot is known as
pinching. It is observed that pinching at 40 days after transplanting enhances flower yield.
However, Giant double African yellow and orange do not require pinching as the plants are
bushy and branching type.
Harvesting: Marigold flowers are plucked when they attain full size. Harvesting should be
done either in the morning or evening hours. Field should be irrigated before 2 days of
harvesting of flowers so that the flowers keep well for longer period after harvest.
Yield:Yield of flowers varies with type and variety. Normally 4-6 ton flowers per acre can
be obtained.
CROSSANDRA (Crossandrainfundibuliformis)
Crossandrais one of the popular commercial loose flower preferred for their bright
colour, light-weight and long keeping quality.
Soil: Crossandra can be cultivated in a wide range of soils. Though fertile, red loamy soils
with pH range of 6 to 7.5 and rich in organic matter are ideal for its cultivation.Avoid
nematode infested soils and high alkaline soils.
Varieties:Lutea yellow, Sebaculas Red, Orange yellow, ArkaAmbara and Arka Shreya.
Propagation:its propagation isthrough seeds or stem cuttings though seed is ideal for its
commercial cultivation.Seeds are sown in May-June in raised beds. About 2 to 2 ½ kg of
seeds is required per ha. The seeds loose viability very soon and hence only freshly extracted
seeds should be used.Treat the seeds with mancozeb or carbendazim @ 2g/kg. To avoid
damping off disease, nursery beds are drenched with wettable ceresin or captan@ 1g/l. When
the seedlings develop 3-4 leaves they are ready for transplanting. The seedlings are
transplanted at a spacing of 60x40cm. Before planting, it is better to dip the roots of the
seedlings in wet Ceresan solution to prevent the incidence of wilt disease. The seedlings will
be ready for transplanting within 50-60 days after sowing. In the case of triploid varieties like
Delhi, Arkaambara,Arkashreya cuttings are used. Cuttings should be transplanted when
sufficient roots have developed.
Preparation of Land: The land is ploughed 4-6 times and ridges and furrows are made at a
spacing of 60 cm and seedlings are transplanted on the sides of the ridges at 40 cm apart.
Manuring:Farmyard manure @ 8 t/acre is applied during last plough. The crop is top dressed
3-4 times with 14-24-24 kg per acre of N: P O : K O each time, at 3,6,9 and 15 months after
2 5 2
transplanting. Application of Zinc sulphate @ 5gm/lat 60 days after transplanting increases
the flower yield and quality. Application of fertilizers is to be necessarily followed by
irrigation.
Irrigation: Immediately after planting, the crop has to be irrigated twice a week and later
irrigation is to be provided at 7-10 days interval based on climate and soil conditions. Dried
flower stalks and branches are to be removed at regular intervals.
Harvest and yield:In Crossandra flowering starts within two to three months after planting
and continues to bear flowers throughout the year with a lean production during rainy
months. Flowers are to be picked early in the morning by pulling the corolla out of the calyx.
Six pickings can be taken in a year. An average yield of 5 to 7 kg of flowers can be obtained
at each picking. Flowers are very light in weight, which accounts around 1500 flowers per kg.
Harvesting of flowers is to be done on alternate days.
Lecture 40
Greenhouse cultivation of flowers -techniques
The technique of providing favorable environment condition for plant growth by means of
controlling temperature, light, relative humidity and other factors to facilitate microclimate
requirement of plants in order to obtain quality produce in a covered structure is known as
greenhouse technology.
Classification of greenhouses: greenhouses are classified based on different factors such as
based on shape, type of cladding material used and environmental control. Considering the
environmental control greenhouses are classified as low cost, medium cost and high cost.
High cost greenhouses are constructed for cultivation of vegetables and flowers for export
purpose. In our region, low and medium cost greenhouses are suitable for successful
cultivation.
Advantages of greenhouse cultivation of crops:
✓ High yield per unit area and superior quality produce free of blemishes.
✓ Possible to cultivate throughout the year.
✓ Offseason cultivation of flowers.
✓ Water and fertilizers are utilized effectively.
Suitable crops for greenhouse cultivation: low volume crops like Rose, Gerbera,
Carnation, Anthurium/ and Orchids.
Planning and design of Greenhouse: construction of greenhouse should be according to the
area and crops to be grown however, it should be permissible ample light required for the
crop.
Orientation: single span greenhouses are constructed in any direction though the multi span
green houses are constructed in North -South direction only to avoid shadow of the structure
at one place.
Parts of green house:low cost green houses consists of frame and roof whereas in medium
cost green houses in addition to these, environmental control equipment/s are also there
which involves additional cost. Generally, Green house frame lasts for 15-20 years, roof for
3-6 years and control/monitoring equipment for 5-10 years depends on the management and
quality.
Types in green house construction: there are two types of construction.
1. Single span green house: this a single unit and can be of any shape i.e., Quonset, gothic,
gable, dome. These are constructed in 100-500 m2.
2. Multi span green house: gutter connected multi span ridge and furrow greenhouses are
suitable for cultivation crops which are similar environmental conditions.
Construction of green house:
a. fabrication of frame:according to size and durability mild steel or galvanized iron pipes
of 0.5 -1.5 mm diameter are used for frame. Cost of these are lesser than aluminium angles.
In low cost green houses, temperature requirement is met by providing ventilation in natural
way hence height should be of 3.5 m for 100 m2area , for the greenhouses of 500m2 or more
5-7 m height is required. Ventilation is provided by employing top and side ventilators.
Polyhouse area of 100 m2 is sufficient for propagation unit and for cultivation of flowers on
commercial scale 300 -500 m2 area is sufficient.
b. frame cladding/roof:different cladding material like glass, fibre glass, polythene are used.
However, U.V stablilized polythene of 200 microns (800 gauge) are suitable.
c. environmental control system:for natural control of temperature, to provide ventilation of
60-70%, side ventilators are arranged with 40 mesh net and upon the need roll up polythene
film should also be arranged. In medium cost green houses, temperature controlling is carried
by providing evaporative cooling system by exhaust fans and cellulose pads.
Management of green house environment:
a. Temperature control: day and night temperature should be controlled based on the
requirement of crop.
Cooling of greenhouse:if the inside temperature exceeds than the tolerance limitsof crop it
should be cooled. It is achieved by
a.Natural ventilation:it works on the physical phenomenon that warm air is less dense and
rises which creates small pressure differences between outside and inside the house and the
inside air blows out. For natural ventilation 20-50%floor area should be provided.
b. Forced ventilation: in this ventilation is achieved through mechanical means by
employing fans, lowers and vents.Lowers are works manually or mechanically. Mechanical
lowers are also helps in protection of greenhouses especially during high windy time.
c. Exhaust ventilation: in this system arrangement is made for installation of more number
of inlets. In single span green houses air movement of 30 m and in multi span houses it
should be of 60 m. fans are fitted at one end and the inlets are arranged on the other end.
2. Roof shading: it is a process of cooling to reduce the amount of solar radiation which
reaches the plant. By reducing the solar load on the green house, the air temperature
difference is smaller, making the absolute air temperatures inside the green house closer to
the outside temperature. Traditionally, it is done by applying a semi permanent shading
compound like
1 kg white lead/ Zinc/ Tilanium paint
1 kg whitening, 41/2 spoons linseed oil, 8 l gasoline or naphta paints (to control fire)
Another way of shading is achieved by attaching a black polypropylene mesh screening on
the outer glazing. Shading can be obtained from 30-92%. internal shading works in similar
way of shade curtains.
3.Evaporative cooling system:it works on the principle of evaporation. In this, fans and pad
are arranged on opposite walls. Fans should deliver required air at 15 mm static pressure. The
maximum distance between two fans should be of 7.5 m. height of fans should be determined
based on the plant height which is proposed to be grown. Fan blades and frames are to be
made of non-corrosive materials like aluminium / stainless steel.
The cross fluted cellulose pad is preferred. These are available mostly in 100 mm thickness.
One meter of pad height is given for every 20 m of pad to fan distance. However, the fan to
pad distance should not exceed 60m. the air flow rate should be of 75 cubic
meter/minute/sq.m of pad. Water flow rate should be of 9 l/min/linear meter pad. Uniform
distribution of water on pad is to be maintained.
4. Water and nutrient management: crops cultivated ingreenhouse required less water
when compared to outside crop. In green house water is applied through drip or micro
sprinkler system. It also facilitates for supply of fertilizers through drip which are applied
from fertigation tanks based on the need of the crop.
Lecture 41
Importance of preservation of fruits and vegetables – important
considerations
India ranks 2nd in production in fruits and vegetables. Though the export share of fruits and
vegetables is <1 % and annually it is around 150 mt. 30-35% of the produce is getting lost
before it reaches to consumers due to improper storage, lack of awareness on scientific
technology. Preservation of fruits and vegetables deals with minimization of spoilage,
processing, storage and preservation of the products for future uses.
Importance of preservation of fruits and vegetables:
❖ Fruits and vegetables are perishable in nature. There is a need to preserve them to
utilize for more days.
❖ Most of the fruits available in one season.
❖ Preservation of fruits is necessary to utilize them in off season too.
❖ It is possible to supply fruits, vegetables and their products from production areas to
non-production areas if preservation is done.
❖ It is also possible to get higher price when there is demand in market during off
season through proper storage of the produce obtained during on season.
❖ Higher foreign exchange can be earned from by products prepared from fruits and
vegetables.
Reasons for non-development of preservation of fruits and vegetables:
❖ Lack of scientific knowledge on preservation of fruits and vegetables.
❖ Non availability of sufficient quantity of fruits and vegetables for preservation.
❖ Higher cost involved in preservation process i.e., machinery, cans etc.
❖ Lack of awareness on government subsidies available for storage, processing etc., to
the farmers.
❖ Lack of transport facilities and marketing system for preserved products.
❖ Non availability of ample quantity of raw material to supply for processing industries
due to non-production of fruits and vegetables throughout the year.
Reasons for spoilage of fruits:
❖ Improper harvesting, packing and transport of fruits.
❖ High temperatures
❖ High respiration
❖ Due to some enzymes like pectinase, hydrolytic
❖ Spoilage due to yeast and bacteria
❖ Due to catalytic activity of enzymes which enhances ripening and also reduces the
quality of fruits.
Control methods for spoilage of fruits:
❖ Higher respiration rate is reduced by storing the fruits at cool temperatures.
❖ Hot water treatment followed by fungicidal treatment (0.1%) reduces the fungal
infestation in humid areas.
❖ Yeast growth can be checked and controlled by syruping fruits at 60-65%
concentration (sugar).
❖ Spoilage bacteria not only spoils the product and also causes swelling, leakage of
the containers and gives offensive odour which can be reduced by pasteurization.
❖ Bacterial growth is arrested at pH of 4-7.5 and its growth is stopped in high acidic
pH. By pasteurization at 1000C vegetative growth of bacteria is stopped since for
spores of fungi needs > 1000 C.
Lecture 42
Role of microbes in spoilage of stored food products – other reasons for
spoilage
1. Nonpoisonous spoilage: when the foods are sterilized at low temperatures this kind of
spoilage occurs through yeast and leads to swelling of cans.
2. Poisonous spoilage: this kind of spoilage is due to thermophilic bacteria. Mostly occurs in
pasty materials like sweet potato. There is no swell in cans due to non-production of gases.
Spoilage due to physical and chemical reactions:
1.Biological:it is due to some enzymes present in foods and it can be checked by removal of
excess gas.
2. Metallic contamination:
a). Ferric tannins: tannins present in fruits and vegetables are readily act with the iron present
in containers and gives black colour to the foods.
Example: Grapes, Pomegranate
b). Iron sulphide: proteins present in foods rotten and release Sulphur di oxide further it acts
with acids present in foods and reacts with cans subsequently produces hydrogen gives black
colour to the foods.
c). Copper sulphide: foods react with the containers made of copper changes the food colour.
d). Hydrogen: acids present in fruits reacts with cans and produces concentrated hydrogen,
this gas further reacts with red and purple fruits and spoils. It canbe minimized by using
lacquered cans.
3. Anthocyanins present in fruits and vegetables with various reactionsleads to colour change
of foods.
4. Oxygen present in containers reacts with the acids present in fruits and combines with
hydrogen and leads to deteriorates the cans.
Generally, the canned foods are get spoiled by faulty storage practices. This spoilage may be
occurred with the physical and chemical actions of microorganisms and gives offensive odour
and taste.
3. Swell: Whenthe ends of an apparently normal and perfect can with good vacuum become
bulged is termed as swell or blower. The bulge is due to the positive internal pressure of
gases formed by microbial or chemical action. different types of swell occurs as follows:
i) Hydrogen swell: this is due to the hydrogen gas produced by the action of food
acids on the metal of the can. The food generally remains free of harmful
microorganisms and it is fit for consumption.
ii) Flipper: The can appears normal, but when struck against a tabletop one or both
ends become convex and springs or flips out, but can be pushed back to normal
condition by a little pressure. It may be caused by overfilling, under-exhausting or
gas pressure due to spoilage.
iii) Springer: A mild swell at one or both ends of a can is called a Springer. Which is
initial stage of hydrogen swell or be due to insufficient exhausting or overfilling
of the can.
iv) Leakage: a leakagecan is known as “Leaker”. This may be due to internal or
external corrosion and mechanical damage during handling.
v) Breather: theremay be a very tiny leak in the can through which air can pass in
and destroy the vacuum. In such cases the food is damaged due to rusting of the
can caused by oxygen in the air but still remains fit for consumption.
vi) Bursting: this may be caused by the excess pressure of gases produced by
decomposition of the food by microorganisms, or by hydrogen gas formed by the
chemical action of food acids on the tin plate. In such cases the canned product
cannot be used.
Microbial spoilage:
Flat sour: this occurs mostly in non-acid foods like vegetables and is caused by
thermophilic species of Bacillus, which produce acid without formation of gas. The
product has a sour odour and its acidity is much higher than that of the normal product. It
is not fit for consumption.
Lecture 43
Preservation of fruits at family level – Zero Energy Cool Chamber
Methods of preservation:
Temporary methods:microbial growth can be checked or stopped to certain extent but not
completely. Some measures like do not damage the fruits while harvesting, use of cleaned
containers for storage and straining of fruit juice through germ proof filter are to be taken at
family level.
1. Freezing: storage at lowtemperature increases the keeping quality of fruits and also
minimizes respiration and microbial growth.
Refrigeration 0-50C, freezing 10-140C
2.Removal of moisture: moisture favours the growth of microorganisms hence removal of
moisture helps in reduction of spoilage of fruits.
Drying: moisture can be removed by drying under sun.
Dehydration: moisture removal is by artificial methods.
3. Absorption of water (moisture): by employing salt and sugar solution microbial growth
can be arrested and also removes moisture from fruits.
Sugar – 70% Salt- 15-20%
4.Use of chemical preservatives: So and benzoic acids are used as preservatives. So in the

form of Potassium meta bi sulphate used for colourless foods while Benzoic acid in the form
of Sodium Benzoate is used for preservation of coloured foods.
5. Pasteurization: heating foods at <1000C stops the microbial growth and helps in storage
of foods.
Foods can be stored in air tight containers.
Permanent methods: in this method microbial growth can be stopped completely thereby
foods can be stored.
1. Sterilization: heating foods at >1000C completely kills the microorganisms. This type of
foods are stored in air tight containers.
2. Fermentation:some of the microorganism’s favours for storage of foods.These can be
used in various types of fermentations.
a). Alcohol fermentation:yeast is responsible for fermentation which converts sugars into
alcohol. 14% alcohol acts as strong preservative. Storage of foods depends on the alcohol
percentage. These foods are to be stored in air tight containers.

b). Acetic acid fermentation: 2% acetic acid (vinegar) is used for preservation of fruits mainly
used in pickles and ketchup preparations. In this method, foods are preserved by using

c). Lactic acid fermentation: fermentation is done by lactic acid bacteria mainly used for

Zero Energy Cool Chamber:fruits and vegetables are perishable in nature and the fresh
produce is getting spoilage due to the lack of on farm storage which accounts huge lost to the
farmers. Cold storage can prolong the life of fresh produce, but the cost to buy the equipment,
run and maintain involves high investment. This can be overcome by construction of low cost
zero energy cool chamber which stays 10-150C cooler and retains 90% relative humidity. It
works on the principle of direct evaporative cooling. Cooling effect obtained by evaporation
of water and faster the evaporation, greater is the cooling. Cool temperatures strew
respiration process, allowing fresh produce for longer time and avoid spoilage.
Construction: the zero energycool chambercan be constructed easily with materials like
brick, sand, bamboo, straw, gunny bags etc. it is most effective during the dry season. The
materials primarily used in constructing these chambers i.e. bricks and sand both has great
capacity to absorb and retain water which evaporates slowly and steadily depending on the
atmospheric temperature and humidity resulting in cooling.

Retain nutritive value

Ideal for household storage
Lecture 44
Cottage industries of fruits - Techniques
Certain by products can be prepared from fruits at small and cottage industries. The following
are the different by products:
1. Jam: It is a Product Prepared from pulp of the fruits after cooking with sufficient quantity
of sugar to a reasonably thick consistency. Jam contains 0.5 to 0.6% acid (as per FPO), 68%
TSS and 45% portion of prepared fruit.
Suitable fruits: Mango, Guava, Papaya, Pineapple, Sapota and other pulpy fruits.
2) Jelly: Jelly is a semi-solid transparent product prepared from clear extract of pectin
containing fruit after cooking with sufficient quantity of sugar. Jelly contains 0.5-0.75% acid
(as per FPO), 65 % TSS and 45% portion of fruit juice.
Suitable fruits: Guava, Papaya, grape, oranges, jamun, woodapple and other pectin
containing fruits.
3) Marmalade: It is a product prepared from citrus fruits after cooking pulp or juice of fruits
with sufficient sugar and using shreds of peel as a suspended material. When the product is
prepared from pulp of fruit and is solid in consistency, it is termed as jam marmalade.
Whereas, the product prepared from clear extract of fruit is termed as jelly marmalade.
Suitable fruits: sweet oranges, sour oranges, mandarin oranges
4)Squash: It is a concentrated beverage prepared from juice of fruits after mixing it with
strained sugar syrup and preservative.
Suitable fruits: Orange, Mango, jamun, muskmelon, watermelon and other juicy fruits.
5) Fruit beverages: Theseareeasily digestible, highly refreshing, appetizing and nutritionally
far superior to many synthetic and aerated drinks. They are classified into two groups.
i)Unfermented beverages: Fruit juices which do not undergo alcoholic fermentation are
termed as unfermented beverages.They include natural and sweetened juices, RTS, nectar,
cardial.
Again the juices are two types I) Natural juices (Pure juices) it is the juice as extracted from
ripe fruits and contains natural sugars. II) Sweetened juice, isa liquid product which contains
at least 85% juice and 10 % total soluble solids.
ii) Fermented beverages:Fruit juices which have undergo alcoholic fermentation by yeast
include wine, champaigne, cidar, nira, etc.
Champaigne – grape juice of France
Sherry - grape juice of Spain
Nira – Juice of Date Palm, Toddy Palm
Feni – prepared from Cashew apple
6) Cardial: it is a fruit juice without any pulp and is clear, transparent and shiny.
7) Sherbat or Syrup: It is a sweetened juice with added sugar and aroma artificially which is
similar to that of natural fruits.
POST HARVEST HANDLING OF FRUITS AND VEGETABLES
Canning/ Bottling: Foods which are filled in air tight containers and heated to kill the
harmful microbes is known as canning /bottling. Before canning some of the precautions
have to be taken as follows:
1. Selection of fruits and vegetables: Fruits and vegetables should be firm and fresh, pest
and disease free while, avoid using over ripen fruits/ vegetables and damaged one.
Peeling: it is done either manually or mechanically.
Advantages: 1. Improves taste of the food.
2. Fruits and vegetables absorbs most of the sugar or salt which acts as preservative.
3. Absorbs much of the heat at the time of canning.
Hand peeling – done in irregular fruits like Mango, Papaya with the help of knife
Mechanical peeling – Potato, Beetroot
Peeling by heat – Tomato, Peaches
Lye peeling – done by dipping in caustic soda (1-2%) for 30 seconds to 2 minutes in
Carrot, Sweet potato
Cutting: Pieces of the requiredsize for canning are cut. Seed, stone and core are removed.
Some fruits like plum from which the seeds cannot be taken out easily are canned whole.
Blanching: Treatment of fruits and vegetables with boiling water or steam for short periods
(2-5 min) followed by cooling prior to canning is called blanching. The main purpose
ofblanching is to soften the texture and to enable a greater weight to be pressed in to the
container without damage to the individual fruit.
Advantages of blanching: Blanching loosens the skin and removes gases and sulphides. It
also inactivates the enzymes thus prevents the discoloration by removing undesirable acid
elements.incase of leafy greens it improves colour and enhances taste and aroma by removing
astringent taste and saponins (peas).
Disadvantagesof blanching: sugars and colour of the fruits and vegetables get dissolved in
water. Vitamin C gets lost.
Can filling: Thoroughly washed and sterilized cans are to be used for filling with fruit or
vegetable. Plain cans are generally used. In case of coloured fruits like, black grapes, straw
berries, etc. fruit lacquered cans are employed.
Syruping or brining: The loaded cans are filled with hot sugar syrup for fruit and with hot
brine for vegetables. It improves the taste of the canned product and fills up the interspaces
between fruits or vegetables in the can. The syrup or the brine should be added to the can at a
temperature of 79OC to 82OC.
Syrup- sugar solution (20-55%)
Brine – Salt solution (1-3%)
Lidding or clinching: the filled cans are covered with lid which is partially seamed to the
can by a single first roller action of a double seamer.The lid remains sufficiently loose to
permit the escape of the dissolved as well as free air from the contents and also the vapour
formed during exhaust process.
Exhausting: The process of removal of all the air from the contents before final sealing of
the can is known as exhausting. Exhausting reduces the oxidation of the product, also helps in
better retention of Vitamins especially Vitamin, C. The tendency of fruits and vegetables to
expand or shrivel during heating, the exhaust process will be of assistance in avoiding over
filling or under filling of the can. The other advantages of exhaust process are prevention of
bulging of can when stored at high altitudes or in hot climates. At the end of exhaust the
temperature at the centre of the can should be about 79OC.In case of glass jars, vacuum
closing machines are generally used. The jar is placed in a closed chamber in which high
vacuum is maintained.
Sealing: After exhausting, the cans are sealed air tight by double seamers and the temperature
of the filled cans should not reach be below 740C.
Processing: It means heating or cooling of canned foods to inactivate bacteria. Over cooking
should be avoided as it spoils the flavour and product appearance. Generally, almost all fruits
can be processed satisfactorily at 1000C temperature while, vegetables, which are non-acidic
(except the acidic tomato) required to be processed at high temperatures of about 1150C to
1210C.
Cooling: After processing the cans are cooled rapidly to stop the cooking process and to
prevent stack burning.
Labelling, Storing and Packing: The outer surface of the can should be dried perfectly. The
cans are then labelled and packed in strong wooden cases or corrugated card board cartons, in
standard packings.They should be stored in a cool dry place.
Containers for canning:
Tin and glass containers have so far been successfully employed for canning foods. In recent
years plastic containers and heat sealable pouches are being tried as possible substitutes for
the familiar tin and glass containers. Although the tin containers are more common in use
since these are fabricated readily and are strong enough to withstand processing, they are
light in weight, easy to handle and fairly cheap, they can be handled in highspeed machines.
Glass containers are fragile and require extra care in handling and during processing.
However, they possess advantages over the tin cans, the contents being visible can be easily
displayed and the containers can be used over and over again
Lacquering: Small microscopic spaces are always left uncoated in steel plates with tin.
Further, these may react with the contents of the can and cause discoloration of the product or
corrosion of the tin plate, when corrosion issevere, the steel is attacked and black stains of
iron sulphide are produced. It is therefore necessary to coat the inside of the can with some
material is known as lacquering. This is achieved by lacquers which are two types viz., acid
resistant and sulphur resistant.
Acid resistant cans: Acid resistant lacquer is ordinary gold coloured enamel, and the cans
when treated with it, are called R- enamel cans. These are used for canning fruits and
vegetables of acid group with soluble colouring matter.
Ex: Pineapple, Grapes, Strawberry
Sulphur resistant cans: This lacquer is also of golden coloured enamel, and the cans coated
with it, are called C-enamel cans (Or) S.R Cans. These cans are used for non-acid products
like peas, corn, beans etc.

Lecture 46
Preparationof Jam and Jelly
Fruits are seasonal and these are available in particular season and preservation of fruits is
important to supply during off season. Different kind of by products can be prepared
fruits of which Jam and Jelly are popular among all those.
Preparation of Jam:
Jam is a product made by boiling fruit pulp with sufficient quantity of sugar to a reasonably
thick consistency, firm enough to hold the fruit tissues in position. It can be prepared from
one kind of fruit or from two or more kinds. In its preparation about 45% of fruit pulp should
be used for every 55% of sugar. The FPO specification of jam is 68.5% TSS, 45% of fruit
pulp and 0.5 -0.6% of acid (citric acid) per 100 gm of the prepared product.
Material required:
• Fruits (Apple, Papaya, Guava, Pineapple, Mango, Sapota)
• Sugar -2kg
• Citric acid essence (50 grams)
• Sodium benzoate – 0.1 g
• Glass bottles 3
• Essence 5-6 drops
Preparation:
Selection of fruits: Select just ripe fruits having good colour, flavor and aroma. Unripe
immature fruits should not be used as the product will be tough. Wash the fruits in running
water. Remove stems and leaves, if any. Trim the bruised and blemished portions.
Preparation of fruits: Peel the fruit and remove any stones, seed and cores. Cut the fruit into
small pieces. If the fruit is tough and hard, boil it in water to soften it. Crush the fruit pulp to
form into a uniform thick mass.
Addition of sugar: Amount of sugar is depends on the sweetness of the fruits. To the sour
fruits, add an equal quantity of sugar by weight of fruit pulp and for the sweeter varieties, add
only 75 % of sugar by weight.
Addition of preservatives: Sodium benzoate at 0.1 g and required amount of citric acid to be
added to the product.
Mixing: Mix the fruit pulp and sugar thoroughly and allow the mixture to stand for half to
one hour so that the sugar dissolves in the juice released from the fruit.
Cooking: Cook the mixture slowly with continuous stirring and crushing till the temperature
reaches 105.50C or till the cooking mass approaches the desired consistency. When the mass
has been boiling and has become sufficiently thick in consistency, dip a spoon into it and let
the product run of the sides of the spoon. If the product falls off in the form of a sheet instead
of flowing readily in a single stream, it means the end point has been reached and the product
is ready for filling into containers. The end point can also be determined by cold plate test
and sheet and fibre test.
Filling and cooling: Fill the hot jam into a clean dry jar or can placed on the insulating
material like a wooden board to prevent the breakage of glass jar. Close the filled container
without delay.
Storage: Allow the jar to cool. Store the container in a cool dry place.
Sealing: Pour molten paraffin wax on the closed jam surface to prevent air contact.

Preparation of Jelly from Jam: fruits which are rich in pectin (Guava) are used for jelly
preparation. Fruits are cut into small pieces and are cooked to extract juice. Further the
extracted juice is to cook till it becomes firm and thicker than jam. Finally, Jelly test is
done with brix reading when brix reading is 92%, cooking process has to be stopped and
of 750 g sugar and 60-80 g citric acid and 5-6 drops essence is to be added (if required).

Extension Education- Meaning:
The word Extension is derived from the Latin roots ‘Ex’ meaning ‘out’ and ‘tensio’
meaning ‘stretching’. Thus, the term extension education means the type of education which is
stretched out into the villages and fields beyond the limits of schools and colleges to which formal
type of education is normally confined. In other words, the word ‘extension’ used in this context
signifies an OUT OF SCHOOL system of education.

Definition.
Extension education is the process of teaching rural people how to live better by learning
ways that improve their farm, home and community institutions
The basic concept of Extension is that it is education. the education is the production of desirable
changes in human behavior.
Extension is providing education. The three kinds of behavioral changes produced through
extension education are illustrated below:
1. Change in knowledge
Eg: Extension worker can improve knowledge of paddy farmers on WTO through trainings.
Eg: Knowledge of rural women on pesticide hazards can be improved by giving trainings
2. Change in skills (Mental and physical).
a) Mental skills: Application of knowledge in solving the problems of life i.e ability of the
person to work out solutions and ways to meet new problems.
Eg: Calculation of seed rates, fertilizer dosages, pesticide dosages etc.
b) Physical skills: Ability of a person to do any work physically
Eg: Skills of women farmers on mushroom cultivation can be improved by demonstrations.
Eg: Skills of farmers on poison bait preparation for Spodoptera management can be
improved by demonstrations.
c) Change in attitude:
Eg: Attitude of farmers can be changed from paddy cultivation to flower cultivation
through exposure visits
Eg: Negative attitude of women farmers towards mushroom consumption can be
changed by explaining nutritional importance to them.
Change in attitude is most important one usually neglected. Extension worker may
improve knowledge and skills of farmers in SRI method of paddy cultivation but unless the
attitude of farmers is made positive towards SRI, implementation does not happen.

2. THE CONCEPT OF THE EXTENSION EDUCATIONAL PROCESS
The earlier concept of education aiming at improvement in Knowledge, Attitude, Skills
happens step wise in a cyclic manner which is termed as Extension Education Process.
The concept of Extension Education Process was developed by Dr. J. Paul Leagans.
According to him, extension education takes place as a process, the education starts with study of
present situation and identification of problems based on the problems identified, solutions are found
out and objectives are formulated. In the third phase, plan of work is taught on how to attain the
objectives, the entire process is evaluated and tested whether formulated objectives are attained or not

ctives, the entire process is evaluated and tested whether formulated objectives are attained or not

and in the final stage reconsideration about the unattained objectives and unaddressed problems and
reasons for not attained.
Extension works undertaken in villages follows the same path.

The first phase is analysis of the situation. This phase requires a large amount of facts about
situation, interests, education, needs, their social customs, habits and folkways, type of
farming, markets size of farms, cropping systems housing, community services and
communications.
The second phase is deciding upon objectives. It is necessary to distinguish between general
objectives from the specific objectives, the planning process must enable the people to select a
limited number of problems and to state their objectives clearly. The solutions to be offered
must give satisfaction. objectives should express the behavioral changes in people as well as
the economic or social outcomes which are desired.
The third phase is teaching. This involves choosing the content or what is to be taught and
methods and techniques of teaching we must use from six to nine different methods of teaching
to stimulate learning.
The fourth phase is evaluation of the teaching. This should determine to what extent
objectives have been reached. This will also be a test of how accurately and clearly the
objectives have been stated. The process of evaluation may be simple and informal or it may be
formal and very complex.
The fifth phase is reconsideration:
After evaluation has taken place. This step consists of a review of previous
efforts and results which reveal a new situation. If this new situation shows the need for further
work, then the whole process may begin again, with new or modified objectives hence this
process is continuous.

Operational leader: These persons who actually initiate action within the group regardless of whether
or not they hold an elected office
Popularity leader: Means in a group a popular person will be elected to a position of leadership
because the members like him sometimes such individual may or may not be the actual leader of the
group, such persons holding elective positions do very little about initiating action for the group and
are mere figureheads as ornamental leaders They are also called ornamental leaders and they are also
called nominal leaders
Assumed representative type: Refers to a person selected to work with a committee or other leaders

work with; he may or may not be a leader of the group (Group A)

Democratic leaders: The leader discuss with the group members about the decisions and planning he

crowd, and He is often a rationalist
